A recent satellite photo captured an underwater cloud of fish sperm, or milt, appearing to glow green during a Pacific herring spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along the coast of Canada's Vancouver Island.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada [48.95586624, -125.42994277]

What's in the photo? A green cloud of milt (fish sperm) and eggs during a Pacific herring spawning event

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This surprising satellite snap shows a giant underwater plume of fish sperm that seems to glow green beneath the waves. The colorful cloud appeared during a spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along Canada's western coastline.

The striking sight was spotted in Barkley Sound, along a section of the southern coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, roughly 45 miles (70 kilometers) north of the U.S. border. The bright-green cloud is the most concentrated between Salmon Beach — the triangular town in the center of the image — and the smaller Forbes Island, which is also "glowing" along its northern coast.

The green cloud is around 4 miles (7 km) from end to end and is made of milt — a fluid containing sperm made by fish, mollusks and other aquatic animals — that was released during a Pacific herring (Clupea pallasii) spawning event. Like many other fish species, Pacific herring reproduce by congregating in large groups. The females lay eggs, which stick to kelp, sea grasses and rocky surfaces, before the males release their milt, which disperses over the area and fertilizes the eggs.

Pacific herring, which grow to around 10 inches (25 centimeters) long, often congregate in this spot off Vancouver Island in late winter or early spring, gathering for several weeks before releasing their gametes, or sex cells, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

"The herring spawn is a really fabulous time to be out here," local resident Ryan Cutler, who used a drone to capture close-up photos of this year's spawning event (see below), told CBC News. "It's a really, really spectacular time to be around."

The cloud of milt arguably looks even more imposing up close, as you can see in this drone photo from resident Ryan Cutler, who described the spawning event as "fabulous" and "spectacular."

Spawning events can last anywhere between a few hours and several days, and scientists are increasingly turning to satellite images to help monitor these occurrences, according to the Earth Observatory. In this case, the milt cloud was visible for around 48 hours.

While the milky substance appears a striking green in these images, it is actually white. It appears green only because it is closer to the surface than the surrounding seafloor, meaning that less reflected light is absorbed by the water. This is also why shallow patches of water often appear turquoise when viewed from above.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The coastline alongside Salmon Beach is perfect for herring to spawn because it strikes the perfect balance between a number of important factors. "Herrings prefer spawning locations that are more protected, have rocky substrate, and allow them to select areas with reduced salinity," Jessica Moffatt, a biologist with Vancouver Island's Island Marine Aquatic Working Group, told the Earth Observatory. "Barkley Sound hits the 'sweet spot' in many of these regards."

The Pacific herring is an important species in this region; it is a primary food source for Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), which give Salmon Beach its name. The herring are also hunted by local First Nation groups, according to CBC News.

During the spawning events, a wide range of other predatory marine life — including large fish, whales and sea lions — are drawn to the area to feast on the herring, according to the Earth Observatory. And on land, eagles, wolves and bears are more likely to appear during the mass reproduction event.

The milt appears green from above due to how wavelengths are absorbed by water as light reflects off the the white substance.

Coincidentally, this exact patch of ocean was the site of one of the weirdest oceanographic events ever seen. In 2020, around 4 miles (7 km) off the coast of Ucluelet (located just along the coastline to the left in the photo), scientists detected a rogue wave that appeared in the open ocean seemingly from nowhere. The massive wave reached the height of a four-story building, making it the most extreme version of this phenomenon ever seen.

Farther offshore, around 150 miles (240 km) south of Vancouver Island, researchers also detected a surprise swarm of more than 2,000 underwater earthquakes in a single day in March 2024, hinting that a section of the seafloor was ripping apart.

A recent satellite photo captured a series of clouds sculpted by von Kármán vortices from a volcano on South Korea's Jeju Island. A giant multicolor plume, ejected by China's Yangtze River, is also visible in the image.

A recent satellite photo captured a gleaming halo of phytoplankton encircling the remote Chatham Islands. The stunning sight is the result of a hidden underwater structure, which has also helped kill hundreds of cetaceans.

A recent satellite photo captured a stunning scene of sediment swirling across the West Florida Shelf after an extreme cold snap that covered large parts of the eastern U.S. in snow.

He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. #6330. In 1969, lightning struck Apollo 12 twice during launch, but the crew reached the Moon and brought back a camera tied to a germ myth

Lightning hit Apollo 12 twice in its first minute in 1969. The crew still landed next to Surveyor 3, whose camera later sparked controversy.

The Apollo 12 moon mission lifted off at 11:22 a.m. EST on November 14, 1969, into a dark, rainy sky over Florida. Thirty-six seconds later, the commander saw a bright flash, and many of the spacecraft’s electronics went offline.

Lightning had struck the rocket. Sixteen seconds after that, a second event knocked out the spacecraft’s guidance system.

The crew still landed on the Moon five days later, right next to a robotic probe that had been sitting there since 1967.

What they brought back from that probe started a story that has never quite gone away: that Earth germs had survived on the Moon.

The crew was commander Charles “Pete” Conrad, command module pilot Richard Gordon and lunar module pilot Alan Bean. Their mission was NASA’s second Moon landing, four months after Apollo 11.

Later crews carried living cargo on purpose, like the tree seeds an Apollo astronaut flew around the Moon in 1971.

A NASA photo shows a bolt between the clouds and the ground 36.5 seconds after liftoff, when the vehicle was about 6,000 feet up. The first event took the spacecraft’s three power-generating fuel cells offline.

The Saturn V rocket that was guiding the launch was not affected and kept flying normally. The spacecraft on top of it was another matter.

In Mission Control, a young engineer named John Aaron was watching the spacecraft’s systems. His data turned to garbage during both events.

Aaron had seen similar readings in a test a year earlier. He concluded that a unit called the Signal Conditioning Equipment had suffered some upset and gone offline, and that a seldom-used switch needed to be moved from Normal to Auxiliary.

He told Flight Director Gerry Griffin, and the call went up to the crew through capcom Gerald Carr. Bean remembered that the switch was on his panel and flipped it. Several seconds later, Aaron had good data on his screen again.

Once Conrad understood what had happened, he radioed Houston: “I think we need to do a little more all-weather testing.”

For about two and a half hours in Earth orbit, the astronauts and Mission Control checked that every system still worked. Then Carr told them they were go to leave for the Moon.

On November 19, Conrad and Bean landed the lunar module Intrepid in the Ocean of Storms, about 950 miles west of the Apollo 11 site.

They came down about 535 feet from Surveyor 3, an uncrewed NASA lander that had been on the Moon since April 1967. It is the only time Apollo astronauts landed near another spacecraft and touched it.

On their second moonwalk, on November 20, the two men walked into the 650-foot-wide Surveyor Crater. They cut off the probe’s 17-pound TV camera and also collected its motorized scoop, pieces of cable, aluminum tubing and glass.

Engineers wanted the camera to see how its gears, motors, optics, metals and lubricants had held up.

Scientists were most interested in the cable, because biological organisms had been trapped inside it, and they wanted to know if any had survived two and a half years on the Moon.

After splashdown, the camera went to NASA’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston. Sampling for microbes began on January 8, 1970.

A team took 33 samples from 11 locations inside the camera body. One sample, a bit of polyurethane foam used as insulation between the aluminum plates of a circuit board, grew a colony of Streptococcus mitis, a bacterium that commonly lives in the human mouth.

The result was published in 1971. It gave rise to the idea that Earth bacteria had survived the vacuum and the extreme temperatures of the Moon, and that idea has circulated ever since.

The broader question is still studied today, as in research on whether Earth microbes can survive in hidden pockets on the Moon.

Decades later, John Rummel of East Carolina University, Judith Allton of NASA’s Johnson Space Center and Don Morrison reviewed the case. They tracked down the 16mm films of the sampling and watched them.

Their review, now hosted by NASA, lists several problems. No viable microbes were found in 10 of the 11 sampling locations inside the camera, or in 32 of the 33 samples.

None were found in the Surveyor cables or in any Apollo lunar samples, and a test camera that had stayed on Earth never yielded S. mitis.

S. mitis is not a spore former, and microbes like it are much more vulnerable to heat, even in a vacuum. NASA’s Manned Spacecraft Center, now Johnson Space Center, estimated that the camera reached a maximum temperature of about 158 degrees Fahrenheit (70 degrees Celsius).

There was also no negative control to check whether the sampling itself added microbes. And S. mitis was one of the organisms found on the crew during routine microbial testing.

The films showed technicians in short-sleeved scrubs, with their arms exposed. Just before the foam was sampled, one worker leaned his upper body into the laminar-flow hood and examined the side of the camera where the foam was.

Morrison concluded that his breath could have contaminated the foam. Because the foam was the last sample taken, nobody could check whether nearby surfaces had been contaminated too.

“The general scene does not lend a lot of confidence in the proposition that contamination did not occur,” Morrison wrote.

The review does not prove where the bacterium came from. What it shows is that the claim of survival on the Moon rests on a single sample taken under weak controls.

The authors used the case as a warning for future missions that bring material back from Mars and other worlds.

Contamination should be avoided but anticipated, and a microbial inventory should be taken before launch. Other scientists have since proposed a Moon lab to screen samples for alien microbes.

Their summary also admitted something about the story’s staying power. Just because scientists do not believe it, they wrote, does not mean it is going to go away.

The information was obtained from NASA’s account of the Apollo 12 launch, its mission summary and the review of the Surveyor 3 microbe claim.

#6329. A meteorite older than Earth crashed through a Texas woman’s roof and landed near her daughter’s bed

The 4.5-billion-year-old meteorite that pierced a home in Spring, Texas is now on free display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science.

On the afternoon of March 21, 2026, Sherrie James heard a thunderous boom at her home in Spring, Texas, north of Houston. A rock from space had just come through her roof.

Eight months later, that rock is on display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science, in a free exhibition called Fall To Earth that opened on November 6.

On the day it fell, it pierced an upstairs bedroom and came to rest near her daughter’s bed. It was a meteorite about 4.5 billion years old, dating back to the birth of the solar system.

James was not the only one who noticed. People across Texas heard a low boom and felt their houses shake, under clear skies, according to the museum.

NASA’s analysis says the meteor became visible 49 miles above Stagecoach, northwest of Houston, at 4:40 p.m. Central Daylight Time. It moved southeast at about 35,000 miles per hour and broke apart 29 miles above Bammel, just west of Cypress Station.

The space rock that entered the atmosphere weighed about a ton and measured about 3 feet across, NASA estimates. When it broke apart, it released energy equal to 26 tons of TNT. That created a pressure wave that reached the ground and caused the booms.

More than 180 eyewitnesses reported the fireball, from as far away as Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin and Rockport, the museum said.

According to NASA, the Geostationary Lightning Mappers on the GOES weather satellites also detected it, and Doppler weather radar showed meteorites falling to the ground between Willowbrook and Northgate Crossing.

Radar has helped track falls before, as researchers showed when they found that weather radar systems can detect meteorite falls.

At first, nobody knew what had hit the house. The Ponderosa Fire Department initially looked into whether the object might be debris from an aircraft.

Its unusual weight and appearance soon pointed to something else. Most of the original space rock burned up before it reached the ground, but some pieces survived.

By late October 2026, 19 meteorite fragments had been recovered around the Houston area, according to the museum.

Researchers at Rice University have proposed naming the meteorite “Houston” as part of its formal classification, which still needs approval from the Meteoritical Society.

It is not the first time a meteorite has hit a home in the United States. A similar rock crashed into a man’s house in Georgia.

Within 24 hours of the fall, experts and enthusiasts were finding small chunks on public property, Rice University said. That is rare: meteorites seldom land in a major city, and samples are seldom collected so soon after landing.

Rice scientist Bidong Zhang walked 23,000 steps searching but found no samples himself. Two other searchers, David Gonzales and Marc Fries, found several pieces and donated them to Rice.

Those samples became the first meteorite tested and catalogued by Zhang’s new Rice Astromaterials Research and Exploration lab, known as RARE.

The analysis confirmed that the Houston meteorite is a chondrite, a type of stony meteorite. Its oxygen isotopes matched what scientists call high-grade H chondrites.

But there was a mystery. Chondrites usually contain small round grains called chondrules, and the Houston meteorite had none.

The scientists found clues in a mineral called feldspar, which was in an unusual sodium-rich form. That suggests the rock was heated to nearly 1,100 degrees Celsius (about 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit) while it was still part of its parent asteroid, hot enough to melt the chondrules.

At some point after that, a high-speed impact likely broke up the asteroid and set the meteorite free. “We think this meteorite was impacted in space,” Zhang said. “It truly is a unique specimen.”

Some results are still unexplained. The levels of one oxygen isotope varied within the samples, when scientists would normally expect them to be fairly consistent, and the team says more work is needed.

The museum calls it one of the most remarkable, documented meteorite falls in recent Texas history. Because the rock dates to the birth of the solar system, it offers scientists a rare chance to study material older than Earth itself.

“A 4.5-billion-year-old fragment of our solar system’s original formation crashed through the roof of a Houston-area home,” said Carolyn Sumners, vice president of astronomy at the Houston Museum of Natural Science. “That’s not something you expect to happen in your own neighborhood.”

James sees it in a more personal way. “That little thing has traveled by planets and stars, there’s no telling how far it’s come,” she said. “So, it’s very exciting. I just feel blessed it came to see me.”

Fall To Earth is free and open to the public at the museum, at 5555 Hermann Park Drive in Houston.

The information was obtained from the Houston Museum of Natural Science, Rice University and NASA’s fireball report.

In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear," author and environmental historian Peter S. Alagona looks at the models used to develop the U.S. grizzly bear recovery program, and how California could make an ideal home for a new population.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are.

But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet" (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out.

Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. They assume that conservation efforts should focus on the best remaining grizzly habitats, and that we can best understand those habitats by studying bears in the places where they still live.

The result has, indeed, been a far better understanding of grizzly habitat use. But this approach has also produced a circular logic with a structural bias toward the status quo. In most grizzly habitat models, past realities and future possibilities fade. With each new study, it seems more and more like the only possible places for grizzlies are the exact kinds of places where they currently live.

The six recovery areas identified in the 1993 Recovery Plan were all places where grizzlies still lived or had recently lived when they were listed as threatened in 1975. The plan argued that these areas "had the potential to provide adequate space and habitat to maintain the grizzly bear as a viable and self-sustaining species." But it also acknowledged the risks and uncertainties facing the bears, and it pledged to assess other areas in their historical range.

This process was expected to take five years. Twenty-eight years later, in 2019, the FWS settled a federal lawsuit in which it agreed to finally conduct this long-delayed analysis. It built a simple model based mainly on secure habitat, and then applied it to both the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and the Sierra Nevada of California. Other potential recovery areas — such as the North Rim of the Grand Canyon in Arizona, the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico, and the Northwest Forest of Northern California — were, for unexplained reasons, not included.

The current grizzly bear recovery zones with the proposed boundaries.

The model did its job. According to the FWS, neither the San Juans nor the Sierra Nevada contained enough secure habitat to support a viable grizzly population. Instead of subjecting the study to peer review, the FWS published it in an appendix on page 286 of a species status report. Having pioneered the idea of secure habitat, David Mattson now set out to explain why the FWS was abusing it. In his view, the service's models focused on artificially small areas, failed to consider several key factors described in the scientific literature, and neglected to conduct essential supporting analyses to explain its conclusions.

The FWS had dragged its heels for almost three decades, and then, after pledging in court to conduct a good-faith analysis, produced a study that seemed designed to reach a predetermined result: The only places capable of supporting grizzlies were the places where the FWS was already trying to recover them. When Mattson and his colleague Troy Merrill ran a more detailed model for the southwestern states, they found that Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah contained seven potential recovery areas with more than 45,000 square kilometers of suitable habitat that could probably support more than 1,000 bears.

For more than a century, the prevailing narrative in California has been that the grizzly's extinction there was inevitable and its recovery is impossible. But Mattson's results for the southwest, combined with California's unique geography, cast doubt on this story.

California is home to nearly 40 million people, and it has more miles of roads than any state except Texas. But its population is extraordinarily concentrated. California is the most urban state, with 95% of its residents packed into cities and 75% living on only around 2% of its land area. Much of California has a human population density lower than that of the Northern Rockies. Unlike in the Northern Rockies, the majority of California's farms are concentrated in broad valleys dozens of miles from core wilderness habitats.

Kings Canyon National Park in California has been identified as one of the locations where grizzlies could thrive.

Outside urban and agricultural areas, California has more protected land than any state except Alaska, including the largest areas of potential grizzly habitat outside the six current recovery zones. Some of these protected areas are in desert ecosystems not suitable for grizzly bears, but others are in mountain ecosystems with potential grizzly habitat.

California's national parks and wilderness areas sometimes strain under heavy visitation, but the numbers paint a complex picture. Consider the southern High Sierra. In 2024, Sequoia Kings Canyon National Park, which is around 865,000 acres and 97% wilderness, topped 2 million visitors for the first time, whereas Yellowstone, which is around 2.2 million acres and 90% wilderness, received almost 5 million visitors, meaning that both parks had about 2.3 visitors per acre. Yellowstone has more than double the total land area in wilderness, but both parks border large U.S. Forest Service wilderness areas and other public lands, and the High Sierra has fewer roads cutting across its protected areas.

In 2024, I coauthored a study, almost eight years in the making, looking at potential grizzly habitat in California. This project, led by Alex McInturff from the University of Washington, ran four computer models, and then compared them to assess the results each produced. One of these models focused on historical sightings of grizzlies in California, two used approaches developed in other regions where brown bears currently live, and one looked at the habitat use preferences of one of California's other large carnivores, the puma.

The Grizzly Bear Recovery Program was created in the 1970s to restore populations to self-sustaining levels.

Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. None of them fully account for the distribution or abundance of food on the landscape or for possible conflicts with people. Together, however, they provide a first assessment of the amount, quality, and locations of potential grizzly habitats. Amazingly, about a third of California appeared as suitable habitat in all four models.

The biggest areas of high-quality habitat were in the southern Sierra Nevada, around Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, where some of the last California grizzly sightings occurred in the 1920s. The Northwest Forest, along the Pacific Coast near the Oregon border, also scored highly owing to its low human population density and rich forest habitats. The Transverse Ranges, in the state's southwestern corner, scored highly because of their rich chaparral habitats and density of historical sightings, but ranked somewhat lower than the other two because more people live, work, and grow crops, including extensive vineyards and avocado orchards, around its borders.

These results made intuitive sense, given the state's robust historical grizzly population, large areas of protected habitat, and healthy black bear populations. But they represented a departure from the conventional wisdom that dominated the circular logic of most habitat models. For the first time, it was clear how much potential habitat could be available in California for a grizzly recovery. But our approach still clung to the conservative assumption that the grizzly is a wilderness species. We had shown, with some important caveats, that California probably had enough wilderness to support one or more viable grizzly populations.

What we hadn't shown was whether Californians were willing to coexist with grizzlies that might, someday, wander outside the state's wilderness boundaries.

From the book START WITH A BEAR: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet, by Peter S. Alagona. Copyright © 2026 by Peter S. Alagona. Published by HarperOne, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Excerpted by permission.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

A century ago, prevailing wisdom cast large carnivores as adversaries—pests and threats to be removed for human safety and prosperity. In North America, among the most targeted of these animals were brown bears, or grizzlies, whose population decimation has made them emblematic of this fear-driven approach to wildlife management.

In California, where they once roamed the land in the tens of thousands, grizzlys have not been seen in more than 100 years. Modern conservation has evolved, yet it often remains rooted in a separation from nature, a systemic opposition that keeps the wild at arm's length.

In Start with a Bear, historian, ecologist, and bear expert Peter Alagona suggests we must reimagine the very heart of conservation, inviting a new framework for sustainable, reciprocal relations with the wild creatures that remain.

Peter S. Alagona is an environmental historian, conservation scientist, and nature-culture geographer. His work explores what happens when people share space and resources (their habitats) with other species: how we interact with non-human creatures, how we make sense of these interactions, why we fight so much about them, what we can learn from them, and how we might use these lessons to foster a more just, peaceful, humane, and sustainable society. He is a professor of environmental studies at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is the author of "After the Grizzly" and "The Accidental Ecosystem."

#6327. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6326. Dust left by an exploded star holds clues to its final hours

Webb’s new view of Cassiopeia A reveals how dust from a supernova can preserve clues to what happened inside the star before it exploded.

Today’s Image of the Day from the James Webb Space Telescope shows a cloud of debris left behind by an exploded star.

Bright orange strands form a loose ring, with wisps of green along the edges and patches of pale blue scattered through the cloud.

The debris stretches about 10 light-years across.

This is Cassiopeia A, the expanding wreckage of a massive star.

The light from its explosion reached Earth more than three centuries ago.

Astronomers are now using dust in the wreckage to investigate a much shorter span of time, possibly just a few hours in the life of the star.

Cassiopeia A lies about 11,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

From Earth, the debris appears roughly circular. Within that outline are strands, knots, and clouds of material that took different paths to get there.

Some came from deep inside the star and were hurled into space when it exploded. Other material had already escaped while the star was alive.

One of the features astronomers examined is a structure nicknamed the Green Monster.

It contains dust rich in magnesium silicates and traces back to material shed before the explosion. Two other regions contain debris expelled in the blast.

One is dominated by silica dust and the other by carbon dust. A single image brings those different pieces of the star’s history into view.

As the blast expanded, it pushed into gas around the star. That encounter produced a second shock wave, called a reverse shock, that traveled back through the outward-moving debris.

As the shock encounters clumps of material, it heats them.

Warm dust gives off infrared light, which Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument can detect.

The orange, green, and blue in the image represent infrared light rendered in colors our eyes can see.

The shapes are what first draw the eye, but the chemistry comes from examining how the dust emits light at different wavelengths.

Different kinds of grains leave different signatures. With Webb, astronomers can examine individual clumps that would have blurred together in earlier observations.

Some of those clumps are roughly the size of our solar system.

Late in a massive star’s life, nuclear fusion can take place in several layers at once.

One layer may be hot enough to fuse oxygen while another, farther out, fuses carbon. Material circulates within each of these layers.

Under some conditions, that motion can carry material across the boundary between them until the layers begin to mix. Astronomers call this a shell merger.

A team led by Tea Temim of Columbia University found signs of that mixing in dust across much of Cassiopeia A.

The Webb observations build on X-ray measurements from NASA’s Chandra observatory and the Japan-led XRISM mission.

Together, the observations support the idea that the oxygen- and carbon-burning layers were already mixing when the star’s core collapsed.

That process may have begun mere hours before the explosion.

NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope helped the team decide where to look.

In a side-by-side comparison of Spitzer and Webb images, the older view catches the broad sweep of the glowing debris.

Webb resolves that same patch into narrow threads and individual knots. That difference matters when two clumps close together in the sky contain different kinds of dust.

By studying them separately, astronomers can trace where those differences occur across the remnant.

Some of the material scattered by supernovae can later become part of other stars and planets.

If two layers mixed before the blast, they could change the mixture of elements the explosion sent into the galaxy.

The dust still glowing in Cassiopeia A gives astronomers a way to connect what the star released with what was happening deep inside it just before it came apart.

Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University). Image processing by Joseph DePasquale (STScI).

#6325. Weight-loss drugs have become more common, but not everyone has access

A study of more than half a million privately insured adults found that where patients received care was linked to whether they filled a prescription for weight-loss drugs.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold as Wegovy and Zepbound, and the two weight-loss drugs can seem to be everywhere.

Only 8.5% of eligible adults in the study filled a prescription for either drug within six months. Patients were more likely to fill one if they received care in areas where more residents had a college degree.

This gap grew as the drugs became more common.

Private insurance was held by every one of these patients. Coverage alone was therefore not enough to make access equal.

The study was led by Minh Trung Le, a research data analyst at Boston University School of Public Health.

He was based in the school’s Department of Global Health. Le worked with Andrew Stokes, an associate professor of global health at the school.

Insurance billing records were used for the analysis. Such records can show a pattern in who received a prescription. The cause of that pattern cannot be shown by them.

Stokes said insurers pay for these drugs far more readily when a patient has diabetes.

He called people with overweight or obesity “a population that has been left behind.”

The records were drawn from a national database of insurance claims. More than 175 million people are covered by that database.

From it, Le and Stokes selected adults between the ages of 18 and 64. They first met the study’s eligibility criteria between July 2021 and June 2025.

Clinical guidelines decide who qualifies for the drugs. The bar is a body mass index, or BMI, of at least 30. A BMI of at least 27 is also accepted alongside a weight-related condition.

High blood pressure and sleep apnea are two examples.

People with type 2 diabetes were excluded from the study. People on Medicare or Medicaid were left out as well, along with those without insurance. That left 512,389 patients.

The researchers checked whether patients filled a prescription for semaglutide or tirzepatide within six months of first meeting the study’s eligibility criteria.

Ozempic and Wegovy are the brand names of semaglutide. Tirzepatide goes by Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Versions labeled for diabetes are at times prescribed for obesity. These prescriptions were included in the count.

The clinics were compared through the ZIP code of each patient’s health care provider. Each ZIP code was looked up in the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey.

The survey reports how many residents hold a bachelor’s degree or higher. On that basis, patients were split into four equal groups.

Among patients diagnosed in the summer of 2021, 1.9% were prescribed one of the two drugs within six months. For patients diagnosed in the spring of 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%.

Even then, about five of every six eligible patients had no prescription after six months.

Semaglutide was approved for weight management by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in June 2021. Tirzepatide got the same approval in November 2023.

Both belong to a class called GLP-1 drugs. In clinical trials, drugs in this class have helped people lose weight. They have also protected the heart.

Both drugs were in short supply at times during the study. When semaglutide was scarce, tirzepatide prescriptions rose quickly. The reverse was seen when tirzepatide was scarce.

Le and Stokes took that as a sign that doctors swap one drug for the other. By the second half of 2024, tirzepatide had become the more prescribed of the two.

At first, prescription rates were about the same in all four neighborhood groups. The rates began to differ in late 2022.

By spring 2025, 21.7% of patients seen in areas with the highest share of college graduates filled a prescription. In the other three groups, the share ranged from 14.4% to 15.2%.

The results were then adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI and other illnesses. The number of doctor visits was taken into account as well.

Between 2021 and 2023, odds of a prescription were 15% lower in the least educated group. The most educated group served as the benchmark. For 2024 and 2025, that figure reached 35%.

Among men, the neighborhood gap was wider than among women. The overweight range showed the widest gap of any BMI category. Odds in the least educated group were 40% lower there.

For the most severe obesity category, the difference shrank to 10%.

Le and Stokes offered a possible reason. More illnesses tend to be on record for patients with severe obesity. An insurer’s approval rules may be easier for them to meet.

By the spring of 2025, 20.7% of women were prescribed one of the drugs. Among men, the figure was 11.9%. After the same adjustments, men had less than half the odds that women had.

Age was linked to prescriptions too. Adults ages 35 to 54 had about twice the odds of adults ages 18 to 24.

Black patients and Hispanic patients each had 11% lower odds than white patients. About a third of the records had no race or ethnicity listed, though. Those two estimates may be shakier as a result.

As BMI rose, so did prescriptions. Even so, most patients in the most severe obesity category went without one. Only about one in five of those diagnosed in the spring of 2025 got a prescription.

Earlier research suggests that early treatment can prevent or ease later complications, Le and Stokes wrote.

Among patients who first qualified in summer 2021, 1.9% filled a prescription for either drug within six months.

By spring 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%. Even then, about five in six eligible patients had no recorded fill within six months.

The forms for that approval are filled in by the staff of the clinic. Fewer of those forms may be handled by a clinic where staff are few.

Cost was named second. Different amounts are charged to patients by different employer health plans for the same drug.

In a 2026 study, 8,914 privately insured adults who had started semaglutide were followed by other researchers.

After accounting for other factors, researchers found that patients who paid more than $168 per 30-day supply were 9 percentage points more likely to fall short of the study’s refill target than those who paid $21 or less.

A review of approval rules and of patient costs was requested by Le. He also asked for help with approval forms for clinics that are short of staff.

Payment programs that reward clinics for quality targets were mentioned in the paper as well. If prescribing rates were made a target, a short-staffed clinic could be penalized for the shortage, not its care.

The ZIP code of the clinic was held by Le and Stokes for each of the 512,389 patients.

The income and the schooling of each patient were not held by them. The study therefore cannot assign the gap to the clinics or to the patients.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold to some people by direct-to-consumer sellers and no insurer is involved.

Sales of that kind are not recorded in claims and were not counted by the researchers. Which groups of patients buy the drugs in this way is not known.

A diagnosis had already been given by a doctor to every patient in the study.

Diagnosis codes are applied unevenly and milder obesity is often left unrecorded, Le and Stokes wrote. Some adults who were eligible may have been missed for that reason.

More than 60 data sources are combined in the database that was used. It was still not described by the authors as a match for all insured Americans.

The cause of the neighborhood gap has not been found. Insurance rules, prescribing habits and patients’ awareness of the drugs were listed by the authors for future studies.

Records of direct-to-consumer sales were also suggested by them, to show who is missing from the claims.

The full study was published in the journal Health Affairs Scholar.

#6324. Amazon’s New 6-Inch Kindle Is So Small, I Bring Mine Everywhere

This tiny e-reader is fast, cute, and built for commuting.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon just gave its Kindle lineup a major makeover, and the smallest model might be the most exciting. Earlier this month, the company introduced a redesigned 6-inch Kindle that's more compact than any e-reader users have seen before. It’s got a sleek new look, faster performance, and four gorgeous colors that make the popular device feel like a cute accessory in its own right. After spending some time with the new Alpine Sky version, I can confidently say that its tiny size is one of my favorite things about it.

The new Kindle is officially Amazon's most pocket-sized e-reader yet, featuring a redesigned flush-front display that eliminates the raised border around the screen. The 6-inch, 300-ppi glare-free display is still black and white, but the device itself now has color that stretches seamlessly from front to back. Amazon also says the new Kindle opens books 30 percent faster than its predecessor and offers up to six weeks of battery life on a single charge, which has been ideal for me, someone who forgets to charge any of his devices.

One of the biggest updates is the introduction of two different versions of the 6-inch Kindle. The standard model starts at $149.99 and comes in Ube (a pretty purple shade) and classic Graphite, with 16 GB of storage. For $189.99, you can upgrade to the new Kindle Aluminum, which comes in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green, with a premium matte aluminum back, 32GB of storage, and no lock-screen ads.

I have the Alpine Sky version, which has a beautiful, soft blue finish that always gets compliments from friends. But beyond the new colors and materials, I've appreciated most how easy this little thing is to bring everywhere. I live in New York City, so I'm constantly taking the subway, and carrying a physical book around isn't always convenient. It’s not impossible, but it can be a nuisance when I'm reading something particularly thick. The Kindle is smaller than most of the books I own, takes up little room in my bag, and feels comfortable to hold for longer reading sessions without making my hand ache.

I also love that I can throw it into pretty much any bag I'm carrying, whether it's a small everyday bag or something much larger. And, admittedly, there's something funny about watching other commuters on the subway notice it. I swear I can see people clocking the tiny blue Kindle and thinking how cute it is (but that could just be my main-character energy). The text is still plenty readable despite its smaller display, and sometimes I feel like the person sitting next to me is following along with whatever chapter I'm on.

Of course, the smaller Kindle doesn't have every feature you'll find on Amazon's pricier models. It lacks waterproofing and adjustable warm lighting like the Kindle Paperwhite, so readers who prioritize those features may prefer the larger option. But if you want a convenient, portable way to read, there's plenty to appreciate here.

The new 6-inch Kindle and Kindle Aluminum are available to shop now, with prices starting at $149.99. Whether you're new to e-reading or just want something smaller for your commute, Amazon's latest release makes a pretty convincing case for carrying an entire library in your bag.

#6323. High school and college teams can win up to $20,000 each by designing technology for NASA’s Moon Base, and sign-ups close January 25

NASA's Moon Base Challenge invites U.S. high school and college teams to design technology for a lunar base.

NASA wants high school and college students to help design the base where astronauts will one day live on the Moon. The agency has opened what it calls a $1 million competition for student teams, and the deadline to sign up is January 25, 2027.

The Moon Base Challenge was announced on November 8 at a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. It is open to student teams at U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools.

Teams do not need prior specialized engineering or technical experience. In the final round, they can explain an idea with a mock-up made of cardboard. Students have helped with real research before, as when students helped astronomers track a rare alien comet.

NASA is building a Moon Base where astronauts will live, work and explore in the lunar South Pole region. The agency says a permanent human presence on the Moon paves the way for future crewed missions to Mars.

The region may contain resources that could one day help support explorers. NASA plans to send a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE to search for evidence of water ice and other resources there.

“We’re looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute.”

“Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we’re looking for,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program.

Each team picks one of six categories: power generation and storage, habitat construction using lunar materials, life-support systems, surface mobility, communication networks, or astronaut safety.

Habitat ideas can go beyond engineering, since researchers have argued that Moon bases could be designed to ease anxiety and homesickness.

The designs have to work in a harsh place. According to the official rules, they must handle vacuum, radiation, micrometeorites, abrasive dust and temperature swings from 248 degrees Fahrenheit (120 degrees Celsius) to minus 274 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 170 degrees Celsius).

They also have to cope with day and night cycles that last two weeks each, and rely as little as possible on supplies from Earth.

Water is one of the hard parts: one analysis found that the Moon can generate enough power for a permanent city, but not enough water.

A team has two to five students and an adult coach, at least 18, who holds a formal role at the team’s school or organization, such as a teacher, faculty member or club advisor.

There are three divisions, judged separately. High school teams are for students in grades 9 to 12 who were between 13 and 18 years old when registration opened, including home-schooled students.

The other two divisions are for undergraduates at two-year schools, such as community and technical colleges, and at four-year colleges and universities.

Those students must be at least 16. A mixed team competes in the division of its most advanced or oldest member. Middle school and graduate students cannot take part.

Students must be U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents or foreign nationals who are full-time students at an eligible U.S. school and physically live in the United States for the whole challenge.

Every student has to create an account on NASA’s STEM Gateway, and only the student team lead submits the application. Coaches should not register there; they are linked to the team later on the organizer’s platform.

In the first phase, teams write a Concept Overview Paper of 5 to 7 pages. It must explain how the idea works and how it survives lunar conditions, and include at least one page of diagrams or other visuals. Papers are due February 22, 2027.

Up to 100 teams will be named finalists on March 11. They will then record a pitch video of up to 10 minutes, with a deck of up to 15 slides, due April 19.

Finalists can explain their design with hand-drawn diagrams, posterboard schematics or low-cost mock-ups made of cardboard, foam or household materials. CAD software and physical prototypes are allowed but optional. Winners will be announced on May 6, 2027.

NASA’s announcement calls it a $1 million challenge, and the challenge website says up to $1 million in monetary awards are available.

The official rules for the 2026-27 challenge, however, list a total maximum prize payout of $500,000, and neither source explains the difference.

Each of up to 100 finalist teams gets $1,400. In the final phase, up to 12 grand prize winners get $20,000 each, and up to 12 runners-up get $10,000 each.

The rules also say payments depend on federal funding and NASA’s final approval, and NASA does not have to award the full amount if too few entries meet its quality bar.

The money goes to a U.S. bank account designated by the team’s coach, who decides how it is shared. Teams keep the rights to what they invent, although NASA may negotiate a license to use it.

A virtual opening symposium introducing the categories is set for December 3. Registered teams can also join live question-and-answer webinars on January 14 and February 11, 2027. The organizers say all dates may change.

The challenge is run for NASA by the Institute of Competition Sciences. Full rules and registration steps are on the official challenge website.

The information was obtained from NASA’s announcement, its Moon Base page and the official rules.

Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.

#6321. Traces of insecticide in cord blood raise new questions about childhood development

A Japanese study linked insecticide exposure before a child's birth to lower scores on certain thinking tests at age nine.

Two compounds linked to widely used insecticides turned up in umbilical cord blood in a Japanese study.

At age 9, children with higher levels of one compound at birth scored lower on a test of processing speed, while those with higher levels of the other scored lower on a test of visual reasoning.

Earlier tests, given between 10 and 32 months, yielded no clear links after researchers accounted for the number of comparisons they made.

The researchers wrote that any association may hinge on the age of the child and the skill examined. Just 200 children took part. Proof that the insecticides caused the weaker scores cannot be drawn from this work.

Abir Nagata and Kenji Tsuchiya, a professor, headed the investigation. Both are based at the Research Center for Child Mental Development at Hamamatsu University School of Medicine.

They are also affiliated with a graduate school run jointly by The University of Osaka and four other Japanese universities.

The growth of a child’s brain and abilities is referred to by scientists as neurodevelopment. Children in earlier work on these insecticides were seldom followed beyond early childhood.

“Previous studies have largely focused on neurodevelopmental outcomes at a single time point,” Nagata said.

Nicotine served as the chemical model for neonicotinoids. Their target is a receptor on nerve cells that normally binds one of the body’s chemical messengers.

Insects carry these receptors and so do humans. Within a fetus, the authors wrote, the receptors assist nerve cells in maturing and connecting.

Harm to bees is what the insecticides are chiefly known for. Over a quarter of global insecticide sales are now attributed to them.

Food and drinking water have both been found to contain residues. Nationwide monitoring in Japan has picked up neonicotinoids in tap water throughout the year.

Animal experiments have been cited as grounds for concern. Altered brain structure followed exposure during brain development in those experiments. Impaired movement, learning and attention were documented as well.

Links with early development have been reported in several studies of children. Agreement between those studies has been poor, however.

All of the children are enrolled in the Hamamatsu Birth Cohort, an ongoing project on child development. The project recruited 1,258 babies. Their births took place in Hamamatsu, Japan, between December 2007 and March 2012.

Urine from pregnant women was the usual source of insecticide measurements in earlier research. What actually reached the baby in the womb is not shown directly by urine. Umbilical cord blood drawn at birth offers a direct measure.

Limited resources meant that cord blood from only 200 randomly selected children could be analyzed. Serum, the liquid fraction of blood, was screened by a laboratory for insecticides and their breakdown products.

Of the ten compounds measured, just two turned up often. Dinotefuran was detected in 104 of the 200 samples, or 52%.

A breakdown product of acetamiprid, a second insecticide, was the other. Its detection rate was 62.5%, or 125 samples.

The team split the children into low, middle and high groups for each of the two chemicals. Detection was seldom possible in the low group, which was used as the comparison.

Quantities were minute. A typical reading in the high dinotefuran group was 0.07 billionths of a gram per milliliter of serum.

The researchers scheduled five rounds of testing between 10 and 32 months of age. Depending on the visit, 185 to 195 children had enough data to be included in the analysis.

Toddlers with higher levels scored below the low group in a handful of comparisons. Large body movements at 10 and 14 months were weaker in the middle dinotefuran group.

The reverse was seen once. Hand and finger skills at 18 months were stronger in the middle group for the acetamiprid breakdown product.

The team ran 50 comparisons per chemical over the toddler period. Some results will appear meaningful purely by chance when that many comparisons are run.

Statistical significance was lost for every toddler result after the researchers corrected for this. Across ages and skills, no consistent pattern emerged.

A standard four-part intelligence test was completed by 178 of the 200 children at age 9. Differences on two of the four parts survived the same correction.

Processing speed was lower among children in the middle dinotefuran group. The measure captures how fast a child gets through simple tasks.

The shortfall against the low group came to roughly 7 points. An average score on this test is 100.

Perceptual reasoning was weaker in the high group for the acetamiprid breakdown product. Visual puzzles and pattern spotting are what this part of the test relies on. The gap on this part was almost as wide.

Overall IQ scores were lower in those same two groups as well.

Rising insecticide levels did not bring a steady decline in scores. Processing speed was also lower in the high dinotefuran group. That difference was smaller, though, and chance could account for it.

Tsuchiya said the contrast with the toddler findings may reflect links specific to certain skills and ages. On that reading, no single lasting pattern runs through childhood.

The children were only observed as they grew up, and nothing about their exposure was controlled. A link can therefore be identified by the study, whereas a cause cannot be proven.

A single blood sample taken at delivery supplied each child’s insecticide level. The timing of exposure during pregnancy cannot be learned from one sample. Neither can the degree to which exposure varied.

Adjustments were made for each child’s sex and age, premature birth and the education of both parents.

Diet went unmeasured, as did lead, other heavy metals and the parents’ own thinking skills. Part of the gap in scores might be explained by such factors.

Dinotefuran levels at birth were also higher in children who took the age 9 test than in the rest. The results could be skewed by that difference.

Too few samples contained the eight other compounds for them to be analyzed, alone or combined.

Only 178 children contributed to the age 9 results. The authors wrote that estimates from a sample of this size are imprecise. Weaker links may also have gone undetected.

Whether other groups of children show the same links is the next question. Why the links would surface at age 9 and not sooner also remains unexplained.

The authors called for larger studies. Exposure would need to be measured several times during pregnancy in such studies. Testing of the children would continue through middle childhood.

For now, a single group of children in one Japanese city is the source of the evidence.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6320. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.
