#6319. The 6 Most Reliable Walkie-Talkies for When You Need Them Most

Stay connected wherever you go with these durable, two-way radios built for everything from backcountry trips to emergencies.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it comes to backcountry safety, there’s no messing around. Serious adventure seekers know it’s best to prepare for their outdoor escapades—whether they’re heading deep into the wilderness or staying close to home. If not, you risk injury or worse. From a reliable fixed-blade knife to a solid pair of binoculars for scouting the trail ahead, there’s a whole slew of gear to keep you safe outdoors.

Used for decades, walkie-talkies are a lesser-talked-about gadget for hikers, campers, paddlers, bikers, skiers, and more heading into the wilderness. Yet this humble piece of equipment plays an important role in helping you communicate with colleagues, friends, and family when you’re on the go. They’re also a smart backup in an emergency and a way to monitor the weather in untamed landscapes and far-off places.

Today’s walkie-talkies haven’t changed all too much in look and feel from their early days. But they’re nothing like the cheap, toy versions we used as kids when exploring backyard “wilderness.” Modern features like NOAA weather alerts, VOX (hands-free operation), and app-connected features provide safeguards and peace of mind—especially in faraway places.

Our guide below covers what to keep in mind and how to choose a walkie-talkie for work, play, and emergencies—and offers a closer look at standout models worth your money.

Our evaluation process combined rigorous field testing across a wide variety of walkie-talkies in different environments with extensive research from trusted online sources. Meehan’s in-field testing for his best two-way radio picks ranged from trekking deep into the backcountry on hut trips to communicating seamlessly while mountain biking to traveling around a city.

Recognizing that walkie-talkies serve a wide audience, we also considered other scenarios where dependable communication is essential—on construction sites, inside expansive venues like convention centers, and across large retail operations.

With this breadth of uses in mind, we reviewed models spanning a range of functions and price points, carefully weighing usability, durability, range, features, and cost. For radios we couldn’t test directly, we reviewed trusted sources and compared specs. We also factored in real-world customer feedback, ensuring our final selections reflect not only expert insights but also everyday user experiences.

These Midland radios have proven reliable in the city and the mountains. The two-pack is a great value and includes advanced features like hands-free VOX and NOAA weather channel monitoring.

It's one of the most versatile walkie-talkies in terms of power options. As part of a two-pack, you get a charging cradle for each, but you can also charge the device with a micro-USB cable and, if you’re in the field for multiple days and run out of power, you can switch the battery pack out for a new one or use three AA batteries to power it—though it is hard to get the cover off.

The radios are compatible with multiple accessories, like a hand-held mic-speaker or an earpiece-mic combo. The latter makes hands-free use even easier, like in a restaurant or store setting.

But in the end, this relatively affordable set of walkies has an ideal feature set for most people.

It shouldn’t surprise that a company known for its smartphones, like the Razr+, would add smartphone-like features to its top-line walkie-talkies. That’s exactly what Motorola did with its 800-series Talkabout line.

It uses the Talkabout app for iOS and Android devices to enable features other walkie-talkies can’t, like letting you use the 800 series as a sort of smartphone modem when there’s no cell service.

The app also lets you send texts or share your location with others using an 800-series radio and the app. This feature is unavailable on most walkie-talkies, since they’re just two-way radios. It also supports smart pairing and connects to Bluetooth devices, like headphones or earbuds.

Most walkie-talkies on the market are waterproof, or at the very least water-resistant, since they’re meant for outdoor use. But you’ll find it harder to find a two-way radio that can actually float. That’s where Cobra's floating walkie-talkies stand out.

Built to IPX7 waterproof standards, this radio can survive full immersion underwater and is designed to float—ideal for situations like water sports, boating, paddling, skiing, and backcountry adventures. This walkie-talkie can handle dunkings and wet environments where communication is critical, and its orange rubber exterior makes it easy to spot in choppy surf or on snow-covered slopes.

Best for whitewater kayakers, stand-up paddle boarders, or even families enjoying a long weekend on the boat, it's a solid pick when you want to stay connected without worrying about waterlogging. You won’t have to worry about sinking or failing when wet. This durability is also ideal for backcountry skiers or climbers who deal with wet conditions daily.

Extra features like voice-activated transmission (aka hands-free talking) and the ability to replay missed radio calls also pack a punch. With its 37-mile range, NOAA weather alerts, and an impressive 2662 channel combinations, this Cobra radio is more than just waterproof—it’s an essential tool for adventurers heading into rugged, remote environments.

In the end, it’s hard to deny the Rocky Talkie Mountain Radio's capabilities compared to others made for outdoor adventure. It could easily have been our top pick, but since not everyone goes on multi-day backcountry trips, the Mountain Radio is likely overkill for most.

Founded in 2019, RockyTalkie is a newcomer to the scene, but it has nailed it with this 2-watt FRS radio with great range. Even in forested, mountainous areas, we could still easily communicate over miles. It also had one of the longest-lasting batteries, even in freezing weather.

The Mountain Radio sports a really simple interface with just five buttons, and it’s easy to lock onto a channel. The radio also has a great speaker and microphone for transmitting and receiving calls and a bright green LED display that disappears when the radio isn’t actively transmitting or receiving.

We also appreciate the radio's rugged, rubberized outer shell and its two removable attachment points. The device uses carabiners rather than belt clips like most other two-way radios. That makes it easy to attach to just about anything—a harness, a belt loop, a backpack strap, a PFD, and more. The secondary attachment point uses smaller carabiners and a coiled leash, making it even harder to drop or lose.

The only thing we found lacking in the radio is that it can’t scan and play NOAA weather alerts, which would be very helpful in a backcountry setting with no access to cell service.

The Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio showcases backcountry endurance at its finest. It’s beefed-up, replaceable battery lasts up to six full days on a single charge. That’s nearly a week of reliable communication without scrambling for a power bank or solar panel to plug into while off-grid—making it one of the longest-lasting walkie-talkies in its class.

This two-way radio also shines for its durability, with an IP67 waterproof and dustproof rating. It also includes NOAA weather alerts, dual-frequency monitoring, and up to 5 watts of transmitting power for extended range. An important note: you need a GMRS license to operate this radio legally in the field.

While its design is compact, it’s heavier than many other walkie-talkies we tested. That said, for the peace of mind that comes with extended battery life and a durable design that tops our list for its rugged, waterproof build, you can’t go wrong with this radio.

Bottom line: the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt is our go-to choice for lasting power and rugged dependability.

While it’s technically not a walkie-talkie, the Garmin InReach Mini 2 deserves a spot in any serious communication roundup. For backcountry adventures where two-way communication is less frequent or a walkie-talkie just won’t cut it, this pocket-sized satellite device becomes a lifeline—especially when cell service and radio coverage fail.

The InReach Mini 2 uses the Iridium satellite network to deliver global coverage wherever you roam. You can send two-way text messages, share GPS location, and trigger SOS alerts from literally anywhere in the world. This piece of tech is best described as a satellite phone stripped down to the essentials: sending and receiving messages without overcomplicating communications.

It weighs a mere 3.5 ounces, and its compact design lets you clip the sat-phone to your pack or strap, or slide it into your pocket. You can also sync the InReach Mini 2 with Garmin’s Earthmate app for easier texting if you have your phone with you on your adventures.

Another big selling point of this piece of gear over walkie-talkies is its 14-day lifespan—long enough for extended off-grid trips. Unlike FRS or GMRS walkie-talkies, which are limited by terrain and line-of-sight requirements, this communication device promises to keep you in touch with family and friends wherever your adventures take you. Even more importantly, it keeps you connected in an emergency.

While a walkie-talkie is a simple, handheld, portable two-way radio, not all are the same. Some are designed for indoor use, while others are meant for outdoor use. Some suit adventurers and sportspeople, while others offer features best suited to first responders. And, of course, some are designed for kids. When selecting the right two-way radios for your needs, there are plenty of factors to consider.

Most walkie-talkies are Family Radio Service (FRS) units with 2 watts or less of broadcasting power. These need no license. Devices that have more than 2 watts of broadcasting power, up to 50 watts, are called General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) units.

GMRS devices require an FCC license. However, as the folks at Rocky Talkie explain on their site, it’s pretty easy to get one online in the U.S. It costs $35 and is good for 10 years, covering everyone in your immediate family. The higher the wattage, the more transmitting power and range the walkie-talkie has, which generally means it uses more power and has a larger antenna. You can see that difference pretty clearly between the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio and the brand’s smaller 2-watt Mountain Radio.

Both types of units can broadcast on a range of channels, and each channel has wattage restrictions. Channels 1 through 7 can broadcast at up to 5 watts. Channels 8 through 14 can only broadcast at up to 0.5 watts. Channels 15 through 22 can broadcast at up to 50 watts, making them ideal for communications up to 30 miles apart in good conditions.

Not all two-way radios are designed with the same level of user-friendliness and a simple interface. The interface plays a big role in how easy the device is to use, especially when in the field with limited bandwidth for fidgeting with buttons and screen controls. Some radios keep things simple with large knobs and backlit buttons that let you seamlessly switch channels or adjust volume with a quick twist or tap—even while wearing gloves. Others rely on small digital menus that can be challenging to navigate, especially while on the go.

And some advanced walkie-talkies even require setup, such as programming frequencies through a computer and cables. While this may give more control, it can intimidate newer two-way radio users.

When comparing radios, pay attention to details like clearly marked buttons, backlit displays for night use, and easy setup processes. Features like one-touch scanning or memory recall can be great options when you need quick, efficient communication. Ultimately, the best radio delivers reliable performance without sacrificing user experience—especially when it matters most in the field.

Most two-way radios use replaceable batteries, usually AA or AAA, rechargeable batteries, or sometimes can use either. Units with rechargeable batteries are often more expensive, but usually have good longevity for trail and backcountry use. Some units recharge in a cradle but ideally also have a port for charging via a DC or USB cable, allowing you to power up from a backup battery as needed. We’ve left units on overnight before and still had power in the morning, and some will go into a low-power mode when left on. The battery will last longer if you use the walkie less or use a lower wattage mode, but that will also reduce its transmitting and receiving range.

Obviously, you want your devices to last a long time, and walkie-talkies should endure for years and withstand knocks and drops. That's why most don’t have touchscreens or even glass screens. Most should be able to withstand minor spills or rain, but if you know you’ll be using them primarily in the water, like on a fishing boat or white-water rafting and kayaking, you’ll want a walkie-talkie that’s waterproof and carries an IP67 rating or higher. If you’re using walkies in the backcountry or on a job site, you’ll want two-way radios that are ruggedized—like the DeWalt 2-Watt Heavy-Duty Walkie-Talkie or Rocky Talkies—and can withstand drops better than some others.

Walkie-talkies offer a few options for remote operation. Some will allow VOX or hands-free operation and are activated by your voice. Others have wired microphones and speakers that are handheld or worn on a lapel or shoulder strap. Others have an earpiece and microphone. Some modern walkie-talkies can actually pair with Bluetooth earpieces, also allowing for hands-free communication. This is great when wearing a motorcycle helmet or when a wire could get in the way of whatever you’re doing.

Some models have additional channel monitoring or communication capabilities, like operating on two frequencies at the same time. These are handy features, but using them will drain the battery faster while they’re on.

Walkie-talkies designed for outdoor use, for example, can monitor NOAA weather channels, giving you some insight into the weather and the conditions you may face while camping, driving off-road, hiking, or hunting that you otherwise wouldn’t be able to access.

Still others can communicate and monitor two channels at the same time. That could allow you to communicate with multiple teams at once. For instance, in a rescue situation, you could communicate with your friends on one channel and the local sheriff’s office or the search-and-rescue team on another without switching channels every time.

While all walkie-talkie channels are open to all users, some are generally used by certain groups and/or in certain areas. You can talk with local organizations to find out which channels they use and broadcast on.

To help people connect with like minds, some are encouraging what they call community channels. These help people in a local backcountry area communicate with each other. Rocky Talkie lists some active community channels for local areas. While these channels help in some situations, you also don’t want to communicate constantly on channels monitored by SAR or local sheriff’s offices, because you could interrupt emergency operations.

Walkie-talkies come in a wide range of prices, and more expensive models often offer more benefits and features. So, while you can get a serviceable pair for about $30-$35, they won’t have much range or additional features. For a top-tier single walkie-talkie with multi-channel monitoring, high wattage and range, and water- and shock-proofing, you can expect to pay over $150 per unit.

Range is one of the biggest selling points for walkie-talkies, but it’s also one of the most misunderstood. Sure, the box may say “up to 35 miles of range.” That’s only if conditions are near-perfect—think one person on a mountain peak and another down in a valley, with nothing but clear air between them. In reality, terrain, obstructions, severe weather (like a snowstorm), and more can drastically cut that range. Dense forest, rocky canyons, massive hills, and buildings can shrink that range even more.

Most consumer FRS models perform best up to five miles, depending on the terrain. For most outdoor adventures, a reliable one-to-five-mile range is typical and usually enough to keep track of groups across rivers, campsites, or trails. GMRS radios, which we mentioned require a license, can stretch much further than five miles, especially when paired with repeaters.

Our recommendation: Shop for a walkie-talkie model and range based on realistic expectations for your use case, not the maximum range advertised in the brand’s marketing.

It depends! How often and for how long do you plan to use your radio? Are you looking for a basic radio or one built to perform off-grid? Battery life depends most on design and how often you use it. Most walkie-talkies advertise a battery lifespan of eight to 20 hours of runtime, but those numbers assume moderate to infrequent use. Continuous transmission drains the battery much faster than standby mode.

For shorter day hikes and quick outings, you won’t have to worry much about your radio lasting more than a single charge. On longer excursions, opt for a walkie-talkie that can be charged via USB-C with an external battery pack, or that uses AA or AAA batteries. Simply put: Don’t trust what the packaging says. Instead, consider how long you plan to use the two-way radio and whether you’ll have a chance to recharge partway through a long adventure.

Many modern two-way radios offer more than basic push-to-talk functionality. NOAA weather alerts are especially helpful for backcountry safety, providing real-time updates on weather patterns and severe storms heading your way.

Another feature to look for is VOX—voice-activated transmission—which enables hands-free use. Paddlers, bikers, and skiers are prime candidates for VOX-equipped walkie-talkies when devices aren’t always easy to grab while in motion.

For simple day-hiking trail use or communicating with your family across the campground, simple models will work just fine. But on bigger adventures like backpacking into the wilderness and remote paddling, investing in a two-way radio with all the bells and whistles gives you peace of mind and the right tools when conditions are worse than expected.

Erica Zazo (she/they) is a Chicago-based freelance writer covering outdoor news, gear, and guides for Backpacker Magazine, Outside, and more. She’s a big fan of urban nature, exploring lesser-known trails and towns, and the Midwest. Follow her adventures on Instagram: @onecurioustrvlr.

Chris Meehan is an internationally published writer, author, and editor with more than two decades of professional experience. He has authored multiple adventure guidebooks with Falcon Guides and his work focusses primarily on the nexus between sustainability and outdoor adventure. He is an experienced gear reviewer, tester, and travel writer who has explored multiple continents.

#6318. Glaciers lose ice faster where they meet lakes, but there’s more to the story

Glaciers that end in lakes lost ice about 65% faster than those that end on land, but climate and terrain explained more of the variation than lakes did.

Meltwater is often collected in the hollow that a retreating glacier leaves behind.

Once such a lake has formed, the neighboring ice can be lost more quickly. The lake melts the glacier front below the waterline, and pieces break off more easily.

The size of that effect has now been estimated across the world’s glaciers by an international team. Between 2000 and 2020, glaciers ending in lakes were found to lose ice about 65% faster than those on land.

In the researchers’ model, lake characteristics accounted for about 11% of the differences in ice loss the model could explain. Climate and glacier terrain accounted for most of the rest.

The work was led by Shaochun Zhao and Guoqing Zhang. Both are at the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Their 15 co-authors work in China, Europe, and the United States. One of them is Tobias Bolch of the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology.

The team worked from satellite images and a statistical model. No instruments were placed at the ice.

Glacial lakes were mapped everywhere outside Antarctica using images from the Landsat satellites. The images were taken around 2000 and again around 2020.

Software trained to recognize lakes drew the first outlines. Those outlines were then checked and corrected by eye.

A lake had to cover about two-thirds of an acre (0.0027 square kilometers) to count.

Glacial lakes of every kind increased 9% in number, to 160,332. Lakes touching a glacier increased 35%, a gain of 3,567 lakes.

Three-quarters of the water added to glacial lakes went into lakes touching ice.

The team estimated that lakes in direct contact with glaciers held about 16 cubic miles (66 cubic kilometers) more water by 2020. Volume was worked out from surface area with the help of depth surveys of 299 lakes.

Bolch’s university put that volume in city terms. Poured over Vienna in an even layer, the water would stand about 525 feet (160 meters) deep.

Worldwide growth of glacial lakes since 1990 had already been documented in the same journal by a 2020 survey.

In that survey, however, lakes were not sorted according to whether they touch ice. That detail was required for the present study.

Expansion of ice-touching lakes by more than 39 square miles (100 square kilometers) was recorded in only two regions. These were Alaska and the southern Andes. Fifteen of the 20 lakes with the largest growth are located in these two regions.

The largest single gain, roughly 20 square miles (53 square kilometers), was measured at a lake in Alaska. Within the southern Andes, growth was concentrated around the two Patagonian ice fields.

Most of the growth came from a small number of large lakes. Although 2,946 lakes expanded in total, 810 of them grew by more than 25 acres (0.1 square kilometers).

Those 810 lakes accounted for 92% of the total area gain.

A further 4,538 ice-touching lakes were formed between 2000 and 2020.

Contact with the ice was not maintained everywhere. During the same period, 1,645 lakes became detached from their glaciers. In New Zealand, eight lakes were detached while only three new ones were formed.

To compare glaciers, the team relied on the Randolph Glacier Inventory, a global catalog of glacier outlines. It was combined with an existing record of glacier ice loss.

Of roughly 214,000 glaciers, 7,121 terminate in a lake and 1,512 in the sea, while the remainder end on land.

Ice loss is expressed by glaciologists as a depth of water. This is the depth the lost ice would produce if spread across the whole glacier.

By that measure, lake-ending glaciers lost about 26 inches (0.66 meters) a year.

For land-ending glaciers the figure was about 16 inches (0.40 meters), and for sea-ending glaciers about 14 inches (0.36 meters).

Bolch was part of a team that found a similar gap among Himalayan glaciers in 2019.

The fastest ice loss was not seen at these glaciers everywhere. In Iceland, Svalbard, the Russian Arctic, and northern Arctic Canada, they lost less ice than land-ending ones.

A possible reason was suggested by the authors. Lake-ending glaciers in those regions are considerably larger and lie at higher elevations.

Over those 20 years, about 1.5 trillion tons (1,362 billion metric tons) were lost by lake-ending glaciers. This amounts to roughly 28% of all glacier ice lost worldwide.

Studies of single glaciers had disagreed about how much a lake matters. At two glaciers in southeastern Tibet, the loss was dominated at certain stages by ice breaking off into a lake.

Studies in the western Himalaya and British Columbia suggested that lakes played a secondary role.

To weigh the causes, machine learning was used. Here, a program learns which measurements best predict an outcome. Three such programs analyzed the lake-ending glaciers.

For each glacier, the lake’s size and growth were recorded together with 20 years of temperature and precipitation data. Slope, elevation, and latitude were also included.

Of the ice loss the best program could explain, 46% was attributed to a glacier’s shape and position. Climate was assigned 43% and lakes 11%.

Each share carries an uncertainty of 7 to 10 percentage points.

Steeper and higher glaciers tended to lose less ice. Glaciers whose lakes grew more tended to lose more.

The lakes’ share was highest in regions where lakes had expanded substantially. It was about 14% to 15% in Scandinavia, Alaska, and the southern Andes, and 5% in northern Arctic Canada.

Bolch ranked the causes the same way, placing climate and terrain ahead of lakes, which “significantly exacerbate” the loss.

Deeper lake water pushes up harder on the front of a glacier, which helps floating ice detach. Lake water also melts ice below the surface.

A glacier’s loss is measured by satellites that track the height of its surface. Ice lost underwater can’t be seen that way.

That uncounted loss was estimated at about 62 billion tons (56 billion metric tons) for 2000 to 2020. If it were counted, the total for lake-ending glaciers would be raised by roughly 4%.

With other volume estimates, that figure reaches as much as 8%.

Water that would otherwise reach the ocean is also held back by lakes. Between 2000 and 2023, melting glaciers added about 0.7 inches (18 millimeters) to global sea level.

By comparison, only a small amount was stored in glacial lakes from 2000 to 2020. The team calculated it as about one hundredth of an inch (0.24 millimeters) of sea level. That estimate assumes all the water in the lakes came from glaciers.

The results should make forecasts of glacier change more accurate, Bolch said.

Mountain regions and the lowlands below them have the most use for such forecasts, Bolch added. A significant share of their water comes from meltwater.

The best program accounted for a little more than half of the differences in ice loss among glaciers. Several of its lake measurements were stand-ins.

Depth matters most right where water meets ice, and direct measurements there are scarce. The team therefore relied on an average depth, which was estimated from each lake’s surface area.

The length of ice touching water came from a single date. The warmth of each lake could only be approximated, using air temperature and lake volume.

Ice thickness at the glacier front wasn’t in the analysis, the authors wrote. Neither was the shape of the ground beneath it.

Anyone assessing the danger of outburst floods from glacial lakes can use the findings too, Bolch said.

Future research could measure water depth and temperature at glacier fronts. How the line where ice meets water shifts over time could also be tracked.

Physical models built for lake-ending glaciers would give a more accurate answer than statistics, the authors wrote. Such models already exist for glaciers that end in the sea.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Climate Change.

Eagles appear to be hunting and killing adult baboons, study finds. Does that mean they could have hunted ancient human relatives?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eagles can hunt exceptionally large prey, including a baboon that weighed nearly 60 pounds (26 kilograms), a new study finds.

Some human ancestors were smaller in size than modern-day humans and weighed around the same amount as the baboons. This raises the question of whether they also might have faced eagle attacks, the researchers said.

Until now, it was thought that eagles couldn't lift nonhuman primates weighing over 29 pounds (13 kg), the researchers reported.

Scientists made the finding while conducting research in the Sahara Desert in Chad. They found the remains of at least nine adult baboons that had been killed recently by eagles. The region is home to Verreaux's eagles (Aquila verreauxii), which hunt from cliff tops, sometimes in pairs, and have talons with a grip diameter of 16 inches (40 centimeters). Grip diameter is how far the eagle’s grip extends.

The scientists found deep talon marks on the baboons' bones. These marks suggest that the eagles hunted and killed the primates and brought parts of them back to their nests, the team noted in a paper published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

The photo on the left shows an eagle-baboon encounter, while another image (right) features a baboon skeleton with marks of eagle predation.

The baboons were sizable, with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kilograms). The largest of them weighed 58 pounds (26 kg), which is similar in size to some small hominins, a group that includes humans and our close relatives that arose after the split from chimpanzees and bonobos, the researchers noted. For instance, the Australopithecus afarensis individual known as Lucy weighed about 62 pounds (28 kilograms) when she was alive in what is now Ethiopia around 3.2 million years ago.

While eagles do sometimes scavenge carcasses, this doesn't seem to be the case with the baboons. The "severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip," the team wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

They noted that eight out of nine of the baboons in the study were male. This suggests that the baboons were hunted, since scavenged animal remains would not favor a particular sex. Why eagles hunted mainly male baboons is not clear, and the "male sex-bias in our sample is puzzling," the researchers noted. Male primates, such as monkeys, do sometimes defend against eagles by charging at them, the team added in a statement.

There is one known example of eagles hunting and killing a hominin. The "only confirmed case is Taung Child, an infant Australopithecus who we think was taken by a large eagle around 2.8 million years ago," study first author Catherine Hobaiter, a professor at the University of St. Andrews in the U.K. who has studied primates extensively, told Live Science in an email. The Taung Child weighed around 22 pounds (10 kg).

Hobaiter noted that "several of the australopithecine species who lived around 1 [million to] 3 million years ago would be in the same weight range as the adult male baboons in our study" and would have been vulnerable to eagle attacks. Other large predators, such as hyenas and crocodiles, also would have been a threat.

Nowadays, smaller primates, such as monkeys, defend against eagle attacks by traveling together.

"Modern primate species that are predated by eagles spend time in mixed species groups — for example foraging together," Hobaiter said. "That means extra competition for the food — but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost."

Hominins may have done something similar, with different hominin species traveling together to defend against eagle attacks, she noted.

An illustration of a Verreaux's eagle hunting an adult male baboon.

Robert Simmons, a researcher at the FitzPatrick Institute of African Ornithology at the University of Cape Town who wasn't involved with the study, called the findings "fascinating." Eagles "are opportunistic — an old male or a young male baboon dispersing to another troop found on its own can become prey to an opportunistic eagle, or a pair of eagles," Simmons said in an email. In a desert region, the lack of cover can leave baboons exposed.

This is "certainly a rare occurrence," he said. But in this dry desert environment, the prey available to the Verreaux's eagles is limited, which has forced them to take on larger, more dangerous prey than is typical for a 9-pound (4 kg) eagle, Simmons explained.

W. Scott McGraw, an anthropology professor at The Ohio State University who also wasn't involved with the study, said in an email that early "hominins may have been particularly attractive targets because of their relatively small body size," especially infants and juveniles.

"Given their limited physical defenses, early hominins — and, indeed, primates more generally — likely evolved a range of behavioral adaptations to reduce their vulnerability to raptors and other predators," McGraw said. These adaptations may have included living in groups, yelling out to warn others, and selecting habitats that could offer protection from attacks.

Jesús Bautista-Rodríguez, the coordinator of the Desert Golden Eagles Project who has conducted extensive research on eagles, said that the finds were interesting but was cautious about some of the conclusions.

"I am much more cautious, however, about interpreting the remains described in this paper as evidence that the eagles actively killed healthy adult male baboons weighing over 20 kg [44 pounds]," Bautista-Rodriguez told Live Science in an email. "In my opinion, it is quite possible that some, or even all, of these individuals were already dead, dying, severely weakened or otherwise unable to defend themselves when the eagles fed on them."

He also took issue with how the baboons died, saying that more fieldwork is needed to better understand how eagles came across the baboons.

“The punctures and extensive scratches observed on the skulls and scapulae are certainly interesting and compatible with eagle talons and feeding activity," Bautista-Rodriguez said. "Nevertheless, these marks do not necessarily demonstrate that the eagle was responsible for killing the animal. They could also have been produced during the handling, dismemberment and feeding of an individual that had already died."

Hobaiter, C., Akpona, T.J.D., Kopp, G.H., Dominy, N.J. (2026). Signs of eagle predation on a 22-kg adult primate. American Journal of Biological Anthropology. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.70377

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6316. When the Work Gets Heavy, Do Your Tires Hold Up? Cooper’s New Discoverer® HT Is Built to Carry the Weight

Evolved from severe-duty all-terrain designs and backed by an up to 70,000-mile Limited Treadwear Warranty, this highway tire pairs interlocking 3D tread sipes with rigid construction to keep your truck or SUV composed on high-mileage trips.

For enthusiasts, tire shopping is an upgrade, not a chore. While the casual driver might treat new tires like regular maintenance, anyone who cares about vehicle dynamics knows that what meets the road defines how a truck or SUV rides, tracks, and stops. It is the single most transformative upgrade you can make to your vehicle. For more than 110 years, Cooper tires have catered to drivers who look past the showroom floor and seek out products that overdeliver on performance, capability, and long-term durability.

And that level of purpose-built engineering is more vital than ever. As vehicles grow heavier and more capable, tires need to do more than simply roll down an interstate. They have to withstand heavy payload demands, sudden weather changes, and unpredictable pavement. Cooper tires are built to that benchmark. Rooted in American engineering and real-world development, Cooper tires are built to an uncompromising standard that live up to their promises. From the rock-crawling STT Pro to the severe-snow-designated Stronghold AT, the Discoverer® family has earned its reputation through real-world testing from Alaskan ice to jagged mountain trails.

The new Cooper Discoverer® HT adapts that rugged all-terrain lineage for long-distance highway cruising, matching heavy-duty capability with quiet, refined composure. While it retains the structural durability to wander down a gravel trail with a trailer in tow, its core mission is maximizing comfort and control across hundreds of miles of open road.

Where many highway tires trade load capability for a soft ride, the Discoverer® HT is engineered to handle both. Straight, reinforced sidewalls provide the structural foundation needed to maintain an optimal contact patch under load. Whether the vehicle is running light or carrying family, gear, and tongue weight, the tire resists deformation, ensuring consistent steering response and predictable roadholding grip in any condition. It’s engineered for drivers whose tires have to hold their own—providing a dependable, hard-working partner that won’t fold when the truck or SUV is pushed to its limit.

Cooper tires also tackle truck and SUV tire performance, with advanced features. Its proprietary 3-D Micro-Gauge Siping incorporates interlocking zig-zag sipes inside the tread blocks. Under heavy braking, sharp turns, or loaded acceleration, these interlocking sipes lock together to stiffen the tread block, to help support responsiveness. Crucially, these sipes run deep into the tread rubber, ensuring that gripping edges are still present to help with traction. That structural integrity backs up an exceptional UTQG treadwear rating of 720 and a 70,000-mile limited treadwear warranty on passenger fitments.

This is the tire for drivers who expect their trucks or suvs to show up for the long haul. Whether that means towing a camper into the backcountry, handling moving-day payloads, or eating up cross-country interstate miles in quiet comfort, the mission remains the same: a single set of tires that balances real-world traction, refined manners, and hard-working capability.

To fit that wide spectrum of work, Cooper offers the Discoverer® HT across 19 passenger sizes covering 16- to 22-inch wheels (with section widths from 245 to 285 mm), alongside 16 light-truck (LT) options engineered with deeper tread grooves and higher load ratings. Backed by a 45-day satisfaction guarantee and over a century of research and development, the Discoverer® HT delivers what Cooper has always stood for: the quiet confidence that the job was done right.

#6315. Physicists have found half the answer to why some materials carry electricity with no loss

In one copper oxide, flickering electron spins drive high-temperature superconductors, and coupling strength sets where resistance ends.

Every wire wastes a little of the electricity that runs through it, which is why a phone charger gets warm. Cool certain materials far enough and that waste disappears.

A family of copper-oxide ceramics become superconductors at temperatures well above the rest, and physicists have argued for decades about why.

For one branch of that family, a team has now matched the strength of one interaction to the temperature at which the loss vanishes.

Electrons in these materials scatter off rapid flickers in the magnetism of the surrounding atoms. The stronger that scattering, the higher the temperature at which the material stops wasting energy.

So, the authors concluded, those magnetic flickers are what pair the electrons up.

That covers only half of the superconductor family, and the half with the highest temperatures behaves differently. So the answer isn’t complete, and the authors said so.

Nigel Hussey, a professor of physics at the University of Bristol who also holds a post at Radboud University in the Netherlands, co-led the work. Caitlin Duffy, now a postdoctoral researcher at the French research agency CNRS, ran the experiments.

“Through measurements carried out at the European Magnetic Field Laboratory in the Netherlands and subsequent careful analysis, we have found the smoking gun which solves part of the equation and explains what causes this perplexing state,” Hussey said.

In a normal metal, electrons bump into vibrating atoms as they travel, and each collision wastes a little energy as heat. In the oldest known superconductors, those same vibrations do something else at very low temperatures.

They nudge electrons into pairs, and paired electrons flow without resistance.

That theory has a useful feature. The strength of the pull between vibrations and electrons shows up in a metal’s resistance above the transition, and the same strength sets the transition temperature. Measure one and you can predict the other.

The copper-oxide materials become superconductors at much higher temperatures, too high for vibrating atoms to explain. Physicists call that temperature Tc.

The leading candidate for a replacement glue has long been the electrons’ own spins, which act like tiny magnets and flicker in step with their neighbors.

What was missing was a measurement tying the strength of that flickering to Tc, the way resistance ties vibrations to it in ordinary metals.

Collaborators at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing grew a thin film of lanthanum cerium copper oxide, one atomic layer at a time.

Along the film, the cerium content changed smoothly from one end to the other. Cerium adds electrons to the material, and the amount sets Tc.

At one end, the film became superconducting at about 25 kelvin, or roughly -415°F (-248°C), which is close to the best this material can do.

At the other end it never did. Between those ends sat 19 distinct compositions, measured across two films grown the same way, so the amount of disorder stayed the same from end to end.

The team patterned electrical contacts along the film and measured its resistance at each position while varying the temperature and the magnetic field.

The field came from a 35-tesla magnet at the High Field Magnet Laboratory in Nijmegen. This is far stronger than the magnet inside a hospital MRI scanner.

A magnetic field bends the paths of electrons. How much the resistance rises in a field depends on how often the electrons scatter and from where.

In these films, the pattern pointed to scattering concentrated at particular spots, and those spots matched the ones where electrons meet the flickering spins of neighboring atoms.

The team then fit the resistance and the field response at all 13 measured positions on one film. Only one number was allowed to change from position to position – the strength of that scattering.

Across the film, as Tc fell from 25 kelvin to zero, that number fell tenfold. Duffy said the field measurements were what made the identification possible.

“Employing some analytical tricks on the data obtained in high magnetic fields, we were then able to identify the dominant source of resistance in this material as scattering off the fluctuating spins,” said Duffy.

“The correlation between the strength of this interaction and Tc then confirmed that the origin for superconductivity in this material is indeed the interaction between the conduction electrons and spin fluctuations,” she added.

One consequence cuts against an earlier idea. Some physicists had argued that the resistance in these superconductors sits at a universal quantum limit.

The scattering strength here varied by a factor of ten across the film, so in this branch of the family, at least, it does not.

Copper-oxide superconductors come in two kinds. Adding electrons, as cerium does here, makes one kind. Removing electrons, which physicists call adding holes, makes the other. The hole-doped materials reach the highest transition temperatures of all.

A tempting guess is that hole-doped materials simply couple more strongly to the same magnetic flickers. However, the team’s earlier high-field measurements on those materials say otherwise.

In the state physicists call a strange metal, their resistance responds to a magnetic field in a way the same model can’t reproduce. No standard picture of electrons as individual particles has yet accounted for it.

“Although electron- and hole-doped cuprates are made from the same cloth, they are stitched together in different patterns,” Hussey explained.

The result rests on one material, measured on two films, and on a model in which electrons still behave as particles with definite paths. The model’s success here is itself evidence, the authors wrote, because the same approach fails on the hole-doped side.

“While we have found the first key ingredient, the task now is to go and find the second,” Hussey said.

What the second ingredient is, nobody has measured. Finding it, the authors wrote, may take an approach that goes beyond the standard theory of superconductivity, or beyond treating electrons as individual particles at all.

The hole-doped materials are where that search has to happen.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Physics.

#6314. Researchers find a clever way to use everyday garbage to make greener cement instead of burning fossil fuels

A review of 211 studies finds refuse-derived fuel could replace coal in cement kilns, but fuel standards and rules still don't line up.

Plastic bags, blended fabrics, and treated wood are hard to recycle, and a lot of waste like that goes to landfill. Cement kilns, meanwhile, burn coal for the heat that turns limestone into cement, a product behind an estimated 8 percent of the carbon dioxide people put into the air each year.

Feeding kilns with processed trash instead of coal could ease both problems at once. A review of 35 years of research finds the idea gaining ground while the basics stay unsettled.

Geethmi Thisakya, a Ph.D. candidate in the School of Civil Engineering and Construction Management at Adelaide University, led the review with her supervisors Navodana Rodrigo, Chamitha Wijewickrama, and George Zillante.

Her subject is refuse-derived fuel. It’s waste processed into something with more heat per pound, less moisture, and more even particles than raw trash. Burning it alongside coal in a kiln is known as co-processing.

“Previous research has highlighted the potential of refuse-derived fuel to turn suitable waste materials into a useful resource rather than sending them to landfill,” Thisakya said.

The team searched the Web of Science database for every study on refuse-derived fuel in cement making between 1991 and July 2025, and found 211 in English. Almost all of that interest is recent.

The earliest paper that fit dates from 1992, and output stayed low until a rise after 2013.

More than 80 percent of the papers were published in the past 11 years, with a peak of 24 in 2023 alone. Forty-eight records, including seven regulatory documents, were read in full.

China produced the most studies, 29 of them, followed by Germany with 21, Poland with 19, and Brazil with 12. Africa and Latin America barely appear, even though the team sees them as places where the fuel could catch on.

The confusion starts with vocabulary. Refuse-derived fuel has a stricter cousin, solid recovered fuel, which has to meet an international standard called ISO 21640.

That standard sorts the fuel into five classes by how much heat it gives off and how much chlorine and mercury it contains.

Refuse-derived fuel typically has no such standard, yet studies and regulations use the two names interchangeably, the review found.

Some papers call the ISO classes “RDF classes” when the standard defines them for solid recovered fuel, and fuel that meets the standard is sometimes labeled refuse-derived fuel anyway. Sometimes that’s deliberate shorthand, since the standardized fuel is a refined subset of the broader one.

For a kiln operator, the muddle isn’t academic. It affects which fuel a plant will accept, what the emissions paperwork says, and what a supply contract means.

“However, our review shows that realizing this potential requires more than simply replacing coal with waste. We need consistent fuel quality, clear regulations and stronger evidence about the environmental and economic impacts,” Thisakya said.

The European Union has the most developed rulebook. Its rules set emission limits for kilns that burn waste fuel, assign the codes that let the fuel cross borders, and ban high-energy waste from landfill.

One rule pulls the other way, however. As Europe pushes plastics recycling harder, the mixed plastics that make up much of the fuel will get scarcer.

Elsewhere the picture is patchy. In the United States the fuel falls under the Clean Air Act and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, which governs waste handling.

Germany separates the two fuel types in law. Poland still classifies refuse-derived fuel as waste, so moving and storing it needs a waste license. Indonesia pays a feed-in tariff to encourage it.

Peer-reviewed work rarely compares how these regimes affect uptake in cement plants, the review found.

Regulators rank what to do with trash in a hierarchy: prevention first, then reuse, then recycling, then “other recovery,” then disposal.

The authors place refuse-derived fuel in that fourth tier, and in the “recover” slot of the circular-economy list that runs from refuse to recover.

Recycling should still come first, the authors wrote. Refuse-derived fuel is a route for the burnable leftovers that landfills would otherwise take. Other routes to cleaner cement, from different rocks to kilns that capture carbon, fall outside the review.

The search covered one database and one language, so studies indexed elsewhere or written in other languages were missed.

The authors wrote that regional work from non-English-speaking countries is the likeliest gap. They also excluded power plants and district heating, which burn the same fuel, so lessons from those sectors didn’t carry over.

Nor does the review settle how much carbon the switch saves. Early life-cycle studies have weighed the trade-offs of replacing coal, but the authors found none built around the specific conditions of a cement kiln.

That analysis is on their research agenda, along with tests of how the fuel performs in different regions and plants.

What the review asks for next is that number, measured for a cement kiln, before the construction sector counts the switch as a saving.

The full study was published in the journal International Journal of Building Pathology and Adaptation.

#6312. Parasite outbreaks in the food supply chain highlight how much public attention hurts bagged salad sales

Google searches for "cyclospora" predicted where bagged salad sales fell during parasite outbreaks.

A food recall looks like a supply problem: bags pulled from the shelf, a gap in the produce case. During six cyclospora outbreaks between 2018 and 2022, stores showed no sign of cutting back on bagged salad, and prices barely moved, yet households bought less of it anyway.

Weekly purchases ran 3.89 percent below normal, on average, across those outbreak and recall periods, and the missing sales added up to roughly $374 million.

Where sales fell depended not only on where people got sick but on where people were typing “cyclospora” into Google.

Xuerui Yang ran the analysis as a doctoral student at The Ohio State University. She is now a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Florida’s Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS).

The dollar figure is an estimate from household purchase records, and the search counts stand in for a region’s exposure to cyclospora outbreak news, not for what any one shopper read.

In an interview with Earth.com, Yang put the main lesson in one line. “News travels through media markets, not state lines,” she said.

Cyclospora cayetanensis, a single-celled parasite first identified in 1993, can live in soil or water for months. It survives the chlorine washes that processing plants run produce through.

Like other kinds of food poisoning, the infection usually brings watery diarrhea, cramps, bloating and a lost appetite, and most people recover on their own.

People with weakened immune systems can become severely ill or stay sick for a long time.

Large cyclospora outbreaks were rare before 2018. That year, reported outbreaks were tied to 1,165 illnesses nationwide, and the numbers have stayed high since. Packaged salads have been implicated more and more often.

Yang’s team picked six large multistate outbreaks from 2018 to 2022. Four of them traced to bagged salad mix. Together, they accounted for 2,157 illnesses, about two-thirds of every outbreak-linked case reported to the CDC in that span. The rest were smaller events.

Recalls followed the 2018, 2019 and 2020 outbreaks. The 2018 and 2020 salad recalls were traced to a single U.S. manufacturer and spread to store brands. The last two outbreaks in the study ended with no recall at all.

Earlier research on food scares measured public attention through news coverage, which is usually counted by state or for the whole country.

Yang’s team used something finer: how often people searched Google for “cyclospora,” week by week, in each of 210 media markets.

Nielsen draws those markets to map which TV and radio stations a household receives, and they follow broadcast signals rather than borders, so one market can straddle two states.

A second index, built from the public Google Trends tool, tracked general searches for salad, lettuce and basil, with outbreak terms filtered out.

The team matched both against weekly purchase records from a NielsenIQ panel of about 46,000 households a year, 12 million household-weeks in all.

The search index behaved the way a news measure should. Spikes in “cyclospora” searches lined up with spikes in news coverage.

During the 2020 cyclospora outbreak, search activity broadly followed where illnesses were being reported, and Illinois and Iowa reported the most.

Searches for “cyclospora” were linked to the steepest declines in purchases, and general searches about salad and leafy greens were linked to much smaller ones.

The authors read that as information working in two directions. News that names the parasite raises alarm, while ordinary searching about salad tends to settle it.

Recalls mattered on their own. A single week of a cyclospora recall cut purchases in affected states by about 3.2 percent compared with ordinary weeks, and recall periods ran 22 to 31 weeks.

Households whose salad purchases included one recalled brand bought no less than usual, but households whose purchases included two or more recalled brands bought noticeably less. One recalled brand, it seems, made little difference; a second one did.

“What people read online shows up in what they put in their carts,” Yang said.

To check that worry rather than empty shelves explained the decline, the team pulled store-level sales records for 2018 and 2020, the two years with salad recalls.

Store by store, across more than 100 million transactions, there was no sign that retailers cut what they stocked, and prices barely moved.

Media markets gave the team a natural test. In the authors’ example, someone in Washington, D.C., watches the same local news as someone in Virginia.

So a Virginia cyclospora outbreak reaches D.C. households even when no contaminated salad was ever sold there.

In states with no reported illness, households that shared a media market with an affected state bought 3.33 percent less salad per week than in outbreak-free weeks. Those households were a small slice of the data, so the estimate is less precise than the main one.

Yang doesn’t read that as a case for softer warnings. “People in unaffected states still bought less salad when they shared local news with an affected state,” she told Earth.com.

“And we don’t see this as a reason for quieter warnings. When shoppers stayed away from affected products, they’re also protecting themselves. What matters is clear, timely information.”

The 2020 outbreak was the biggest in the study, with 771 illnesses across 14 states. Counting the recall that followed, it reached 33 states and more than 190 million people, and it produced the largest loss, close to $190 million.

The bigger outbreak, though, drew the smaller reaction from shoppers.

Purchases fell about 3.1 percent in 2020 against 4.6 percent two years earlier. Furthermore, the 2020 estimate was weak enough that chance can’t be ruled out as the explanation. Searches for “cyclospora” were also lower and more scattered that year.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her about the smaller reaction, Yang pointed to timing. “Shoppers barely reacted until the recall came,” she said.

“Once specific products were named, purchases dropped. 2020 was also the summer of COVID, and that likely pulled attention away from other health news.”

The 2018 outbreaks cost about $79 million, roughly 1.6 percent of a bagged salad market worth about $4.91 billion a year by the industry estimate the authors cite.

Yang’s earlier work put the retail cost of each of two salmonella outbreaks tied to onions above $1 billion. The authors attribute part of that gap to salmonella being a name that more shoppers recognize.

Google searches catch people looking for information online and miss what they hear on TV, on the radio or from a neighbor. Regions that get their outbreak news offline may be underrepresented.

The search data also can’t show what any individual shopper read, so the results describe regions, not people.

The CDC records the date of a first illness, which comes before the public hears anything. So the study measured changes over whole outbreak-and-recall windows rather than the first days of alarm.

This year’s record, roughly 20,000 confirmed cyclospora cases by the CDC’s count, falls outside the study.

Yang said it raises the questions she would like to explore next: how the scale of the outbreak and the shifting information shaped what people bought.

For a shopper standing in the produce aisle in the middle of one, she had plainer advice. “Follow the official alerts,” she said. “Early on, the source information is often unclear, so if you can’t tell where your salad came from, it’s fine to avoid it for a while.”

“Once a product is confirmed, check whether your salad is on the recall list,” Yang said. “Washing won’t effectively remove the parasite.” Cooking, she added, kills it.

The full study was published in the journal Risk Analysis.

Pregnancy and the postpartum period profoundly transform the brain — yet science is only beginning to understand how that transformation can affect a mother's mental health.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Look closely at the medical illustrations used in textbooks to depict the physiological changes of pregnancy, and you'll notice something strange: The bodies often have no heads. Generations of physicians learned to picture the pregnant patient as a torso — a uterus, a placenta, a growing belly — with everything above the neck left blank.

That blank space is not an oversight by the illustrator. It is a faithful map of what medicine chose to study. We need to move on and create a complete picture of what happens during and after pregnancy so we can develop measures to prevent maternal deaths.

For hundreds of years, we have devoted enormous effort to characterizing how pregnancy remodels nearly every organ and system in the body: the cardiovascular changes, the recalibration of the immune system, the metabolic adjustments — most of them orchestrated by hormones the placenta pours into the bloodstream. That knowledge of what is normal is exactly what lets us recognize and treat what is not, from gestational diabetes to preeclampsia. But the brain, one of the most important organs in the human body, was left out altogether.

It wasn't until 2016 that my colleagues and I published the first study showing that pregnancy profoundly and measurably changes the structure of the human brain. That finding, which we described in the journal Nature Neuroscience, became the seed of my lab. In the years since, a remarkable picture has emerged. The brain changes associated with pregnancy and the postpartum phase are more pronounced, or at least occur more rapidly, than those of adolescence — the transformation we usually treat as the epitome of a remodeling brain.

Today, neuroscientists consider the months of pregnancy and the postpartum period to be one of the most plastic periods for the adult brain. These changes are dynamic; some regions shrink in volume during gestation and grow after birth, while others follow the opposite pattern. They are driven by hormones, tracking with the enormous swings in estrogens and other hormones across pregnancy. And they are long-lasting — some of these structural changes persist for years, and preliminary evidence suggests they may last decades. Or, as folk wisdom has long put it, once a mother, always a mother.

For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank.

These findings raise a question I'm asked constantly: Are these brain changes behind the phenomenon of "mommy brain," sometimes called "momnesia"? It is an effect many women report, and it deserves a careful accounting of its possible causes — among them sleep deprivation and the enormous mental and metabolic load of gestating and raising a human being. We are still investigating, but the data so far point in a reassuring direction: These brain changes are not associated with worse cognitive functioning. If anything, it's the opposite: We have evidence that the women whose brains changed the most were the ones who reported greater well-being and, in turn, an easier time bonding with their newborns.

But not every change is benign. The same plasticity that helps a mother adapt can also carry risk. In one of our most recent studies, published in the journal Science Advances in 2025, we found that certain brain changes were associated with a greater rise in depressive symptoms during the postpartum period. And here is the other side of the coin: A highly plastic brain is also a vulnerable one.

During pregnancy and the postpartum period, that same capacity for change makes the brain more susceptible to disturbances. The window that should lead to learning and bonding, for some women, opens onto suffering instead — especially when society fails to support them, when it doesn't recognize this period as a stage in which women need protection and support from their families and institutions.

The brain changes during pregnancy and the postpartum period are more pronounced and rapid than those that take place during adolescence.

The epidemiological data are as alarming as the personal stories behind them. Roughly 1 in 5 women will experience perinatal depression. In developed countries, suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. Let me say that again, because it bears repeating: Suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. And what happens to a mother's mental health does not stay with her — it ripples out to the well-being of her baby, her family and society as a whole. Advancing maternal mental health is urgent, and the first step is to generate the high-quality data that will let us truly understand the brain transformation that accompanies pregnancy and the postpartum period — to describe what happens to mothers on the basis of science, not personal opinion, inherited prejudice or incomplete medical models.

It is a serious problem, but the solution is straightforward ‪—‬ especially now, in the age of artificial intelligence. The tools of modern data science are extraordinarily powerful, but they are hungry ‪—‬ they need large, high-quality, deeply characterized datasets to learn from and make predictions. In maternal brain health, those datasets do not yet exist. We have blood biobanks from pregnancy, neuroimaging from postpartum parents, questionnaires on bonding, records on breastfeeding — but they sit in separate silos, captured at different moments, never integrated. No resource follows the same women from before conception, through pregnancy, and years past birth, linking biofluids, neuroimaging, neuropsychological assessments, and the social conditions of their lives.

Building that resource should be a priority for anyone who cares about women's health. It is the kind of infrastructure that transformed other fields. Databases like the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative for Alzheimer's disease and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study for adolescence turned scattered observations into predictive science. Motherhood deserves the same — not a footnote appended to the study of something else. It deserves its own chapter — its own public, longitudinal, well-characterized database, spanning from molecules to societies.

For the past nine years, my lab's efforts have focused on laying the groundwork for such a database, and we now have hundreds of participants assessed before pregnancy, during pregnancy, and in the postpartum period. But hundreds is not enough. To do this science properly, we need to scale from hundreds of women to thousands and to ensure, as much as possible, adequate geographic and social representation. My role within initiatives like ENIGMA-Neuroendocrinology and the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative is to coordinate with other outstanding researchers to reach that goal with the highest quality and the greatest urgency we can manage.

None of this requires a scientific miracle. It requires a decision to treat the maternal brain as something worth studying with the same rigor and the same resources we devote to every other domain of biomedicine. For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank. What we need is the collective will, and the sustained funding, to finish the picture.

If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org.

Eighty-five percent of women experience pregnancy at some point in their lives. It enables the very existence of our species. Yet this first step in the process of nurturing the next generation has had little serious, rigorous study — until now.

Susana Carmona's A Mother’s Brain is a landmark in ending sexual bias in women's health. Among her many initiatives, she is building a unique longitudinal database tracking how mothers’ brains change from preconception to several years after childbirth.

Susana Carmona is the author of "A Mother's Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution" (The MIT Press). Carmona is the founder of Neuromaternal, a lab based in Madrid, and is a mother herself. She has led international research projects and published her findings in Science Advances and Nature Neuroscience, among many other publications. Her research has been referenced across popular media from the CBS sitcom "The Big Bang Theory" to the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Washington Post, National Geographic, Smithsonian, and Mother Jones.

#6309. Tiny changes in your pupil size and blinking rate reveal how hard your brain is working

An eye tracker in a VR headset can determine how hard people are concentrating by reading how pupil size changes.

A person’s concentration level during a difficult mental task shows up in the eyes. Pupils open wider and blinks come faster, and a VR headset with an eye tracker inside can record both.

A team in England asked whether a virtual reality headset could use those signals to tell when a person with chronic pain is working too hard. The answer was mostly yes for healthy volunteers, and not yet for the patients.

Jordan Tsigarides of the University of East Anglia‘s School of Health Sciences led the study, which was part of his Ph.D., with colleagues at UEA and the University of Southampton.

Virtual reality is already used as a drug-free way to ease pain, he said. His goal is a headset that changes what it shows, based on how a patient is coping.

“Imagine putting on a VR headset that can recognize when you’re becoming mentally tired or overwhelmed and automatically adjust the experience to suit you,” Tsigarides said in an interview with Earth.com.

“On a difficult day, it might simplify an activity or guide you through a calming environment.”

The study tested only whether the headset could read the effort. It didn’t treat anyone’s pain.

Between March and June 2025, 84 adults put on a consumer VR headset with built-in eye tracking and played a memory game.

Half had lived with musculoskeletal pain for at least three months, most often rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis or fibromyalgia.

The other half were healthy university students and staff. They were younger on average, 35 years to the patients’ 58.

Letters appeared one at a time on a gray panel, each for three-quarters of a second. At the easiest level, a player pressed a button when a letter matched the one just before it. At the hardest, the match was four letters back. The whole session lasted under 20 minutes.

Players found it hard, and said so. Their own ratings of effort kept climbing through the top level, even after their scores had stopped getting worse.

Pupils widened as the levels got harder, by about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) at most, which is less than the thickness of a credit card. Blinks came more often too.

Both changes showed up in people with chronic pain and in people without it, and pain and fatigue scores made no difference to either one.

“What fascinated me was that people’s eyes responded to mental effort in remarkably similar ways, whether or not they lived with chronic pain,” Tsigarides told Earth.com.

A plain average of pupil size told a computer almost nothing. A simple model that used average pupil size alone to sort the easiest level from the hardest guessed right 56 percent of the time in healthy volunteers.

In patients it managed 51 percent, which is barely better than chance. The pattern was in the way the pupil changed second by second, not in its size.

Machine learning models that read the full, second-by-second trace did much better, at least in healthy volunteers. Tested on people they had never seen, the best models picked the easy level from the hard one with 88 percent accuracy.

In the chronic pain group, the same models managed 58 to 65 percent.

Age didn’t explain the gap. When the team matched volunteers and patients by age, or adjusted for it, the patients’ eyes were still harder to read.

The two groups also differed in education, medication and other illnesses, and the authors said a sample of 84 can’t untangle all of that.

The patients were a varied group. Nearly all had two or more long-term conditions, and 45 percent took opioids. A quarter had dry eyes or another eye problem. None of those factors, on its own, predicted whose eyes the models misread.

“Rather than expecting one algorithm to work for everyone, we may need headsets that learn how each individual responds,” he said.

One result was encouraging. People with chronic pain rated their motivation above 90 out of 100 at every level of the game, the same as the healthy group. Motion sickness scores were low in both groups, and pain scores didn’t rise during the session.

Tsigarides holds an honorary chief medical officer role at Revolve Labs Ltd, a company that helped fund his Ph.D. The paper discloses both.

Virtual reality for pain has so far been a fixed experience, Tsigarides said: everyone gets the same woodland walk or the same puzzle, however they feel that day.

His earlier work tested VR therapy in people with fibromyalgia, and he said this study is a step toward a version that adjusts itself.

Everyone was measured once, on one day. The researchers can’t say whether a patient’s eyes behave the same way on a good day and a bad one, and Tsigarides says investigating that question comes next.

“Someone’s ability to concentrate might be very different on a good day compared with a day when their pain or fatigue is particularly severe,” he said.

The team also wants to move from a letter-matching game to the kind of calming scenes a real therapy uses, where changing light levels will complicate the pupil readings.

All of the models in this study were run afterward on a desktop computer rather than live inside the headset. None was tested on an outside group of patients.

Tsigarides told Earth.com he hopes early adaptive systems can be tested within a few years. Whether a headset that reads mental effort and responds to it actually eases anyone’s pain is a trial that hasn’t been run.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#6308. One of the world’s rarest fish lives in a single cave in Death Valley National Park, and earthquakes have left it on the verge of extinction

Devils Hole pupfish live in just one cavern of Death Valley National Park. Earthquakes are rapidly pushing this fish towards extinction.

One of the rarest fish on Earth lives in just one place: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert called Devils Hole, part of Death Valley National Park. In the spring of 2025, after two earthquakes shook its tiny home, biologists counted only 38 of them.

The National Park Service announced the new figure in November. Divers and surface counters found the 137 Devils Hole pupfish during a survey on October 10, nearly double the 77 seen in the spring of 2026 and about double the 69 recorded in the fall of 2025.

Devils Hole is a cave about 12 feet wide and more than 500 feet deep. The bottom has never been mapped. The water stays at a constant 92 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius).

Pupfish have been found as deep as 66 feet, but they feed and spawn only on a shallow rock shelf near the surface, where algae grows.

The species has been isolated there for 10,000 to 20,000 years, longer than any other pupfish in the Death Valley system. The region’s caves keep other long records too, like a Nevada cave that reveals 580,000 years of climate swings.

It is the only naturally occurring population of the species, which was listed as endangered in 1967. Biologists from the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service have counted the fish almost every spring and fall since 1972, with scuba divers in the cavern and counters at the surface.

One of the fish’s main threats can come from thousands of miles away. Large earthquakes as far away as Japan, Indonesia and Chile have made the water slosh in Devils Hole like water in a bathtub, according to the park.

Waves can splash as high as two meters (about 6.5 feet) up the walls and sweep the shelf clean. The park calls it a tsunami in the desert, although it is tiny next to the ocean tsunamis that big earthquakes can unleash.

That is what happened in the winter of 2024 to 2025. Two earthquakes, one in December and one in February, set off waves that moved algae, organic material and fish eggs off the shelf.

The spring count in 2025 found 38 fish. One year earlier, the official spring count had recorded 191.

On July 29, 2025, just 21 minutes after a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, waves rippled through Devils Hole, nearly 4,000 miles away. Those waves were only about 10 inches high and removed just some material from the shelf.

Then, after an earthquake in Panama on October 9, 2026, nearly 3,000 miles away, biologists at first saw signs of stress in the fish. On a later visit, they found them in healthier condition.

The team had prepared for a crash like this for years. Pupfish eggs from Devils Hole had been collected regularly to build a backup population at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility.

In 2025, biologists added captive-raised fish to the wild population for the first time. Between March 2025 and February 2026, scientists released 72 of them into Devils Hole. They also gave the fish extra food while the algae grew back.

The fish live an average of only 10 to 14 months. Because of that, biologists believe most of the 137 fish counted this fall hatched and grew up in Devils Hole itself.

“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” said Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds.

“These results reflect the dedication of our scientists and conservation partners working to protect this extraordinary species. While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival.”

The pupfish has survived human threats before. In the late 1960s, a farming operation drilled large wells in the Ash Meadows area, and the water level in Devils Hole began to drop toward the shelf the fish need.

Biologists even hung a floating, artificially lit shelf in the cave as a substitute. The fish never used it.

A federal court halted further pumping in 1971, and the fight reached the U.S. Supreme Court. Its 1976 decision in Cappaert v. United States recognized the water right of Devils Hole as part of a national monument and limited pumping so the natural shelf would stay underwater.

Until the mid-1990s, spring surveys counted more than 200 fish. In the early 2000s, spring counts averaged about 90, and in 2013 the number fell to 35. The cause of that long decline has not been determined.

The new count is an encouraging step, but the park says the population naturally fluctuates and remains highly vulnerable.

It calls continued monitoring, research and habitat management essential if one of the world’s rarest fish is to keep its foothold in a single desert cave.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s fall 2026 count announcement, its spring 2025 update, its report on the Kamchatka earthquake and its Devils Hole page.
