#6268. The 8 Best Cordless Stick Vacuums Are Convenient, Versatile, and Work Well on Carpets Too

These lightweight, easy-to-store models get the job done with multiple attachments and powerful motors.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A cordless stick vacuum has the potential to be one of the most convenient cleaning tools in your home. These lightweight machines make it easy to clean up pet hair from area rugs and hidden dust along baseboards, without having to haul out an upright vacuum or wrestling with a power cord. Most models also convert into handheld vacuums, giving you more flexibility to clean furniture, stairs, and other hard-to-reach spots.

Suction power, battery life, maneuverability, and dustbin capacities vary between models, so the right cordless stick vacuum ultimately depends on your home’s flooring, how much debris you’re dealing with, and the features that will actually make your cleaning routine easier.

We’ve rounded up the best cordless stick vacuums worth considering based on our hands-on experience, with options for everything from everyday maintenance to deeper carpet cleaning.

🔎 Looking for more ways to keep your floors and furniture clean? Check out our stories on the best robot vacuums, the best vacuums for pet hair, the best vacuums for hardwood floors, and the best handheld vacuums.

I’ve spent considerable time researching, testing, and vetting all types of vacuums, so I’ve developed a pretty good understanding of what separates a genuinely useful appliance from one that is just going to take up space in your storage closet. I’ve evaluated a wide range of models, including full-size uprights, canister vacuums, robot, and handheld models vacuums, paying close attention to performance, ease of use, and features that can really make a difference in a your regular cleaning routine.

When testing cordless stick vacuums, we assessed how well each model could handle common household debris, its ability to transition between carpet and hardwood floors, and how easy it was to move around furniture and into tighter spaces. We also looked at the practical considerations like battery life, suction power, dustbin capacity, weight, filtration, and included attachments.

Beyond just how the vacuum cleans, we also considered the overall experience for an owner. Removable batteries, self-cleaning docking stations, washable filters, and easy-to-empty dustbins can also make daily vacuuming less of a drag. The below recommendations are both powerful and dependable for a wide range of cleaning needs and surface types.

The Dyson V15 Detect is the most expensive stick vacuum in our lineup, but if you can stomach the price tag, you’ll get a cordless stick vacuum that (quite literally) leaves the competition in the dust across the board. It delivers top-notch performance on floors and carpets to tackle everything from fine dust and pet dander to larger debris.

Its motor spins up to 125,000 rpm and it comes with two cleaning heads, including an upgraded version of the brand’s “fluffy” head that features a green laser headlight to detect fine dust. During testing, we found that being able to switch from cordless to handheld made it easier to transition from tackling small messes to deeper cleaning sessions.

The auto mode is a nice feature for conserving battery life, as this model only runs for about an hour off one charge. Another highlight is the motorized pet tool.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

The PowerClean FurFinder is a more affordable alternative to the PowerClean FurGuard we recommend, but that doesn’t mean you have to give up useful features.

This cordless stick vacuum is intended for use on a variety of floor types, and the flat-lay construction makes cleaning under furniture much more accessible. The vacuum also stands up on its own which leads to fewer interruptions during a cleaning session.

We love that both the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment come with headlights because it makes it a lot easier to see hidden dirt and debris. The brush roll is a tangle-free design, and the FurFinder is equipped with a HEPA filter for trapping small particles and allergens.

The motor on this vacuum is less powerful than the PowerClean, but it still provides plenty of suction for daily household cleaning.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurFinder Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Since we’re big fans of the Shark AZ2002 Vertex upright vacuum for deep and thorough cleans, it’s no surprise that we like the cordless model in this lineup, too. The brush roll is excellent at pulling hair and large debris from carpets, as well as polishing up your hardwood floors. The cordless stick vacuum features an advertised runtime of 60 minutes.

It also offers a HEPA filtration system and converts to a hand vac, and it also bends at the center of the wand to get around and under furniture. The Vertex comes with plenty of accessories for cleaning a variety of spaces. However, this may not be the best choice if you regularly clean stairs, as the cordless vacuum weighs roughly nine pounds—significantly more than other vacuums we cover.

I have two cats and live with my partner, which means there is plenty of mess to go around, from pet hair and dust to tracked-in dirt. I appreciate all the thoughtful features of the Tineco Station 5 because they make daily maintenance much easier.

Automatic suction adjustment has proved useful on my laminate and tile floors. I can hear when the motor gets a boost of power in a particularly dirty area, and it helps on carpets and area rugs where crumbs and debris tends to get trapped between the fibers. Add to that a green laser light for dust detection and you’ll hardly ever miss a spot.

I particularly like the base station. It has a 2.5-liter capacity, and after two months of using the Station 5, I still haven’t had to empty it. When I dock the vacuum onto the base, it automatically empties the onboard dustbin, cleans the floorhead brush roll, and charges the vacuum. Combined, these intuitive features make for a cleaning routine that is virtually hands-free.

Full Tineco Pure ONE Station 5 Pro Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Even though the Dyson V11 Origin came out several years ago, that doesn’t mean this model has stopped being useful.

The motorbar cleaner head works exceptionally well on carpet, successfully agitating fibers to pull up embedded dirt, dander, and hair. Suction is equally impressive, and there are three power modes depending on the level of cleaning you need. I ran the vacuum on medium most of the time, but I used boost occasionally whenever an area needed the extra attention.

This model doesn’t come with a soft roller brush vacuum head, and while it does work on all floor types, it can be loud on hardwood and laminate. But if your home is mostly carpet, this is a cordless stick vacuum I would reach for.

Full Dyson V11 Origin Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Our tester has a busy household six pets, so there’s no question that she’s regularly cleaning up after her animals. Pulling out the upright vacuum daily isn’t convenient, so she turned to the Levoit LVAC-300 to fill the gap.

This cordless stick vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—and she was able to cycle through each right from the handle depending on how much suction power she needed. She found that the vacuum was able to pick up litter and sand on different surfaces and between thresholds with ease.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but she was disappointed that there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself. The LVAC-300 runs for up to 60 minutes depending on what mode you’re using, and the HEPA filter is a great feature if you have animals.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

I used the Bissell PowerClean FurGuard across my apartment to clean laminate floors, area rugs, carpeting, and upholstery, and I fell in love with several features.

The vacuum lays completely flat, making it really easy to get underneath furniture, and the swivel steering helps guide the FurGuard around tight spaces. Being a pet owner, I appreciate that the brush roll is tangle-free, so I don’t have to cut hair loose as often as I would with a standard, bristled brush roll.

Other highlights were lights on the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment. I was able to see collected dirt and debris that I would normally miss on hardwood flooring, carpet, and furniture. I also like that this model is designed to be self-standing.

It’s hard to come by a cordless stick vacuum that you don’t have to re-mount or set on the ground during your cleaning session. With this model, I was able to stop and start with ease.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurGuard Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We recently got our hands on one of the latest cordless stick vacuums from Shark, and we were impressed by the PowerDetect’s construction. The pole has a hinge in the center and when you release it, the vacuum bends to extend under furniture and hard-to-reach places. Our tester didn’t have to kneel down or adjust angles while he was cleaning thanks to the intuitive design.

Beyond that, the PowerDetect vacuum uses sensors on the bottom of the floor head to discern between surface types, and adjusts suction power when needed. During testing, the motor could be heard transitioning speeds when used on hardwood and shag carpet.

This vacuum also comes with a docking station, which automates the process of emptying out the dustbin. The vacuum itself can’t hold that much debris onboard, so it’s nice having a one-stop-shop for clearing out the bagless canister during a cleaning session. It’s a little heavy for a cordless stick vacuum, but it still gets the job done.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Not every cordless stick vacuum we test ends up in this roundup. However, these other models still perform well and are reliable recommendations:

Levoit Aero Cordless Vacuum Cleaner: The Tineco we’ve included above has more raw suction power, reaching up to 27,000Pa versus the 14,000Pa of the Levoit. However, one of the highlights of the Aero is the 3.5-liter-capacity dust bag in the docking station. Depending on your cleaning frequency, you could potentially go months without having to empty and replace it, and this design is better for keeping dust and dander from being expelled back into the air.

Dyson Gen5Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum: This cordless stick vacuum certainly commands a premium price, and you get a lot of the same features as the Dyson V15 Detect we recommend above, such as an LCD display screen, the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, and pet hair attachments. If you’re an allergy sufferer, you may prefer the Gen5Detect because its filtration system captures particles down to 0.1 microns, while the V15 filters down to just 0.3 microns. Plus, runtime is slightly longer on the Gen5Detect.

The main advantages of owning a cordless stick vacuum are easy portability and storage. But what you trade for the convenience is battery life and runtime. Most models clean from 30 to 60 minutes, but that’s also dependent on what setting you’re using. If you’re running the vacuum on its highest speed the entire time, it might die faster. Be wary of manufacturers’ advertised total runtime because it may represent performance on the lowest setting or using two fully charged batteries, for instance. Battery charging should also be factored in, so plan your cleaning session accordingly so you don’t lose power in the middle of a floor swipe.

Like we mentioned earlier, the dustbins on cordless stick vacuums are significantly smaller than those of an upright or canister unit. You should consider your cleaning habits and the spaces you usually vacuum to find a model that aligns with your needs. If you live in an apartment or are using the cordless vac to supplement your other cleaning supplies, then a dustbin with at least half a liter capacity should do. Some of the models we recommend hold up to one liter of debris, which helps limit the number of trips to the trash can.

Although not a necessity, having a good amount of attachments with your vacuum is especially helpful for cleaning hard-to-reach places or targeting specific issues. Crevice tools pick up dirt and dander from corners and couch cushions, while bristled brushes and motorized pet tools agitate and lift hair and fur that’s been embedded into upholstery.

A good filtration system helps combat allergens such as dust and pet dander that are being kicked up by a vacuum. The best option is a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. A fully sealed or multi-step filtration system also has the potential to trap a wide variety of airborne allergens without releasing them back into your home.

Cordless vacuums are very effective at picking up pet hair, especially models designed with high suction power and specialized brush rolls. Some of the models we recommend include motorized attachments that lift embedded hair from upholstery and carpets. Anti-tangle vacuum heads are also a key feature that helps prevent hair from wrapping around the brush roll. While not all models perform equally, a high-quality cordless stick vacuum is able to handle pet hair just as well as traditional versions.

The lifespan of these vacuums typically lasts from three to five years, depending on usage, build quality, and maintenance. Battery performance plays a major role, since lithium-ion batteries start to lose capacity over time.

Avoiding overcharging and storing the vacuum properly could help extend the battery life significantly. Running regular maintenance like cleaning the vacuum filters and emptying the dustbin completely preserves suction and functionality. Higher-end models often last longer due to better materials and replaceable parts, but either price point has potential to last for years with proper care.

Modern designs are increasingly more effective at cleaning many surface types, including rugs and carpets. Advances in battery tech and general efficiency have allowed for strong suction performance that is comparable to corded models. Adjustable power modes allow for deeper cleaning on thicker carpets, and multi-roller and motorized brush heads agitate fibers to loosen dirt and debris.

Performance may vary depending on the type of flooring. Some vacuums are designed to work on low-to-medium pile carpets, while others are able to handle high-pile. It’s best to consult the listed features and specs of the model you’re considering to ensure it aligns with the flooring types in your home.

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

#6267. U.S. demand for menopause hormone therapy has more than doubled recently

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Since 2023, monthly dispensing to women aged 40 to 74 grew from 2 million to almost 5 million

A woman applies an estrogen patch, one formulation of menopause hormone therapy. A study that finds a large, recent increase in hormone therapy pharmacy dispensing suggests more women are turning to the medication.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, new prescription data suggest.

Monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although the data in the new study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

The new study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

“Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” says Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The new study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

#6266. The amazing Crab Nebula

One of my personal favorite objects in the night sky is the Crab Nebula (M1). It’s No. 1 on Charles Messier’s list, although I don’t think he ordered his objects by how cool they are (a missed opportunity!). It’s not exactly impressive visually in most scopes — mostly a gray blob, or a spiky gray blob in larger apertures — but it’s one of those targets that if you know what you are looking at, it becomes immensely more interesting to observe.

The Crab Nebula burst onto the scene in 1054 C.E., when a massive star in the constellation Taurus collapsed in on itself in a supernova whose light was visible during the day, as documented by multiple civilizations around the world. Its leftover shell of gas and dust has been expanding ever since, and the bright glow is still visible thanks to what remains of the progenitor star: a rapidly spinning neutron star, known as a pulsar. The “crab” moniker stems from a drawing made by the William Parsons, Earl of Rosse, in the early 1840s with a 36-inch telescope, which depicts crab-leg-like appendages, although he later noted that observations through a 72-inch resulted in a view that looked rather different than his original drawing.

Pulsars are some of the most extreme objects in the universe. The Crab Pulsar, which is approximately 12–17 miles (20–28 kilometers) in diameter, spins at a breakneck 30 times per second — once every 33 milliseconds. At magnitude 16.6, it is a very difficult catch, but possible in large (20-plus-inch) scopes on nights with steady skies. It sits only a few arcseconds from a slightly brighter magnitude 15.8 star that guides the way. The pulsar produces a relativistic-speed stellar wind that generates synchrotron radiation, which occurs when charged particles move along curved paths, bent by strong magnetic fields. This is seen across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to gamma rays, forming the main diffuse part of the nebula’s emission. This radiation has a total luminosity some 100,000 times greater than the Sun’s! The pulsar is slowing down gradually as a result of energy carried away by its stellar wind, increasing its period by 36 nanoseconds per day.

The nebula is still expanding, even nearly 1,000 years later, at a rate of 3.4 million mph (5.5 million km/h) — that’s 950 miles (1,527 km) per second, or 0.5% the speed of light! While not noticeable in a single observation, comparing images across several years shows the expansion on very human-accessible timescales.

The Crab’s intricate filaments are what make it so visually stunning in images. These structures are the remnants of the star’s atmosphere, consisting of gases like ionized helium, hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, iron, neon, and sulfur. It’s a moderately tricky astrophotography target to process: In wideband, it has a largely gray interior wrapped in red tendrils, so it is best imaged in narrowband, where it can display incredible, intricate detail that looks well and truly alien. A famous colorful 2005 Hubble image uses narrowband light from oxygen and sulfur and has oxygen-III set as red, sulfur-II as green, and oxygen-I as blue. When I’ve shot the Crab, I used hydrogen-alpha as blue, since it is a similar wavelength to oxygen-I (which are both red in reality) to create an image reminiscent of the Hubble one, much to my delight.

Whether you are a primarily visual astronomer or a high-tech shutterbug like me, the Crab Nebula is worth spending a little time with this month. Take a moment during your observing to realize how incredible this object is. Rising in the evening hours, it will be up all night for you to enjoy. How much detail can you tease out? Can you spot the pulsar?

Molly Wakeling is an avid astrophotographer active in STEM outreach. She has a Ph.D. in nuclear engineering.

Astronomers have found two rare asteroids trailing Neptune in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data. The rocks, called Neptune's L5 Trojans, could illuminate the conditions of the infant solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered two ancient Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune ‪—‬ the first new ones to be spotted in 15 years.

The findings, published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could improve our understanding of the early solar system while reinforcing the Rubin Observatory's potential to unearth new cosmic objects during its brisk scans of the sky.

Trojan asteroids are icy, rocky bodies that dwell in a planet's vicinity but don't orbit it. Instead, these asteroids orbit the sun, following the same path as the planet. Trojan asteroids exist in distinct swarms roughly 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, called Lagrange points 4 and 5 (L4 and L5), respectively, the gravitational tugs of the sun and the planet balance each other, essentially "locking" the asteroids in position, according to NASA.

However, very few Trojans actually hang around for billions of years. Such asteroids are likely planetary building block remnants from the solar system's infancy, and detecting them in the outer solar system can be challenging.

Jupiter's Trojans are the most famous; the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center notes that an incredible 15,000 of these objects have been discovered so far. But some other planets, including Neptune, also host Trojans. In fact, a 2005 study suggested that Neptune has up to 10 times more Trojans than Jupiter. Until now, though, astronomers have spotted only 28 Neptunian Trojans, with just two of these being long-term L5 members.

There are two reasons why it's difficult to detect these rocks. First, the Neptunian Trojans are extremely faint. More critically, for nearly 15 years, the Trojan population's position in the sky relative to Earth has overlapped with the central region of the Milky Way. Consequently, bright background stars have made it nearly impossible to discern the tiny, faint asteroids, Megan Schwamb, the study's first author and a researcher who focuses on how planets and their building blocks form and evolve at Queen's University Belfast, told Live Science in an email.

An illustration of the Jovian Trojans orbiting in front of and behind Jupiter

However, from 2025 onward, the L5 group's position has moved — albeit extremely slowly — away from the galactic plane. This has made the population slightly easier to observe. At the same time, the Rubin Observatory started scanning the entire Southern Hemisphere sky with the world's largest digital camera.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Rubin is pretty uniquely suited to being excellent at discovering Neptune Trojans," study co-author Kathryn Volk, a scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, told Live Science in an email. "The on-sky density of these objects is not particularly high, so having a large field of view helps a lot!" (Rubin has a field of view equivalent to seven full moons, according to the observatory's website.) This, along with the observatory's excellent vision — which allows it to detect objects 100 billion times dimmer than Venus — enabled the discovery of the new Trojans.

The new Trojan observations form part of the Rubin Science Validation Survey, a three-month-long test run that was held in mid-2025 prior to the start of the observatory's flagship decade-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which is now underway. By chance, the Science Validation Survey encompassed the part of the sky containing Neptune's L5 Trojans, leading to the asteroids being photographed within three weeks of the survey's start.

Following the discoveries, the researchers created computer models to determine the asteroids' orbits. These simulations revealed that the duo will continue to tag behind Neptune for a billion years. The results suggest that the asteroids' trajectories have been stable for several billion years, which means the asteroids may have been traversing these routes from the time of the early solar system. The researchers also found a third object in Rubin's data, but it had a stable orbit in only some of their simulations, leading them to classify it as a candidate Trojan rather than a confirmed one.

However, the two confirmed Trojans likely didn't form in place alongside Neptune. The simulations showed that the asteroids' orbits are highly tilted, just like those of the previously discovered L5 asteroids — suggesting that Neptune captured these objects as they were hurtling past.

Determining the properties of both the Jovian and Neptunian Trojan asteroids will help researchers understand what happened during the solar system's infancy, when the giant planets are believed to have migrated to their present-day positions, Volk said.

Schwamb expects the LSST to unveil many more of the hypothesized Neptunian Trojans, especially because it will survey this same patch of the sky repeatedly over the next several months.

Schwamb, M. E., Bernardinelli, P. H., Volk, K., Murtagh, J., 林 H. W. 省. L., Rivkin, A. S., Chandler, C. O., Jones, R. L., Benecchi, S. D., Jurić, M., Kurlander, J. A., Greenstreet, S., Wilson, A., West, M., & Lyttle, R. R. (2026). NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s first view of the Neptune Trojan L5 (Trailing) cloud: Two new long-term stable Trojans. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1010(2), L36. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aead9a

She's also a self-taught space enthusiast, and so loves writing about topics in astronomy, archaeology and neuroscience.

#6264. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#6263. The 7 Best Miter Saws for Cutting Precise, Accurate Angles

These crosscutting models, including our top choice from Bosch, make possible an endless array of woodworking projects.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not too long ago, making precise angled cuts meant using a simple miterbox—a block with precut 90- and 45-degree slots—and a squat little saw with more teeth than a piranha. Those old-school setups still have their place, especially for ultra-clean trim cuts without tearout, but they’ve largely been replaced by the more powerful and versatile miter saw.

When it comes to angled cuts for trim, framing, or furniture, few tools match a good miter saw. A circular blade mounted on a hinged, pivoting arm delivers fast, consistent, and precise cuts at a wide range of angles—something handsaws and circular saws can’t replicate as easily.

The best models combine clean cutting power with accurate miter and bevel adjustments, smooth sliding action, and enough stability to stay precise while cutting dense wood. Features like clear cutline indicators, effective dust collection, and easily adjustable fences also make a huge difference when you’re making cuts all day.

Whether you’re building a garden bed or installing window trim, a miter saw is the fastest way to get accurate, repeatable results.

When selecting potential options for the original version of this article, author Alex Rennie, a former residential and commercial carpenter in New York City, first put together a rough collection of options based on brands and saw types he had found to be most useful to him over the years. After paring that list down, he put each saw through a comprehensive series of tests.

Paul Smith updated this article most recently with the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 18V Sliding Compound Miter Saw, which impressed him during testing. He is in the process of testing more models and will update this article with the results of those tests when they are available. In the meantime, those models are included below as recommended miter saws based on reputation, product specs, features, price point, and online customer reviews.

Unlike most sliding saws that use rails to slide the blade forward and backward, this Bosch miter saw uses an axial-arm mechanism that eliminates the need for rear clearance. This unique design (also used by this Bosch model) allows the saw to take up considerably less space on your workbench without compromising overall cut capacity.

We loved the lever locks that secure the arm in place during transport (although we weren’t as much of a fan of the saw’s hefty 65-pound weight), and the smoothness of the arm, combined with the rubber handle grip, made this an especially comfortable saw to operate.

It’s worth noting that while the clear blade guard (compared to the black of the DeWalt models) provides a clearer view of the cutline, this saw lacks a shadow or laser line feature.

What the Skil 10-inch dual-bevel miter saw lacks in refinement—things like pro-level build quality, multiple bevel detents, and high-end dust collection—it makes up for in capability and cost. At about half the price of most major brands, it delivers consistently clean cuts on a stable, well-constructed turntable.

The motor spins the blade up to 4,800 rpm quickly, so there’s little wait between cuts. In use, cuts were smooth along the rails as I cut through 2x12s, with no tearout or flyaway pieces. The saw is capable of bevels up to 48 degrees left and 45 degrees right—important if you’re making compound miter cuts for things like crown molding. There is a preset detent at 45 degrees left—a common cutting angle—but any bevel angle in between is easily locked down via the rear bevel knob. Even so, it proved accurate across those settings—I had no trouble dialing in compound miters—cuts that employ both miter and bevel cuts—for crown molding that lined up cleanly from both sides.

Ergonomics are a highlight. The trigger sits naturally within the grip, and it’s the only saw I tested that feels equally comfortable left- or right-handed. That might seem minor, but when you’re stretched out on a tricky compound cut, being able to switch hands makes a real difference. Finally, at less than 50 pounds, this saw is no trouble to move around your yard during setup changes or throw in your truck at the end of the day.

This dual-bevel, 10-inch saw packs a lot of power and features into one relatively small and comparatively inexpensive package. With nine positive miter stops and a cutting capacity of 12 inches on the bed, you’ll get up to 500 cuts on a single battery charge.

LED line indicators ensure precision, and a bevel pivot that's as easy to access as it is to operate rounds out this saw's top features. While it's not the most powerful saw, even compared to other cordless options, this one holds its own among the arguably bigger names that populate this list in every other way.

This DeWalt miter saw provides serious power and performance. We found that it maintained speed and power really well during our cut tests, but because it’s cordless, you don’t need to sacrifice mobility when you’re working with it.

The included stabilizer bar ensured that the saw felt sturdy and stable while we cut, and the included LED work light created a convenient, precise shadow line to maximize accuracy. We also appreciated how well the instruction manual walked us through all the different operations, giving us comprehensive instructions on a variety of cuts.

At a little over 50 pounds (without the 20-volt battery, which you’ll have to buy separately) and with a top-mounted carrying handle, this was one of the easier saws to transport during testing. Plus, this saw’s dust port was located on the side, instead of the rear, which made it easier to fit on a smaller workbench.

With dual-bevel capabilities, smooth gliding rails, and user-friendly controls and adjustment knobs, this cordless powerhouse handles everything from 13.5-inch-wide cuts to 6.5-inch-tall baseboards.

This saw won’t be your go-to if you’re working with large lumber. Nothing bigger than a 2x4 is recommended here, but if that type of work isn’t on your horizon, this saw is as easy to maneuver as it is to operate.

Its small size and extremely accurate blade make it ideal for using indoors to cut trim, flooring, and picture framing. And at just over 14 pounds, it’s a breeze to move from room to room as you work. We also like the gooseneck type of LED built into the blade housing for throwing light on your entire cut. And the 64-tooth blade delivers a clean, precise cut every time.

If you believe you get what you pay for, this Makita 8-1/2-inch miter saw makes the case. Tools should solve problems—and this one addresses a big one in its category: size versus capability. A 12-inch saw powers through 4x4s but is heavy and space-hungry; a compact 6-inch is portable but limited. This Makita saw lands squarely in between.

This 40-volt cordless saw delivers corded-level power in a lighter package—roughly 10 to 20 pounds less than larger models—while still handling 12-inch crosscuts. Its forward-facing rails save valuable workspace, letting it sit flush against a wall without the usual rear clearance.

Build quality stands out immediately. The heavy aluminum turntable feels rigid under load, with precise detents that lock in smoothly at common angles—no fighting to find your mark. Preset bevel stops on both sides add convenience, and the front-mounted bevel lock means no awkward reaching over the saw.

Makita also includes dual dust collection options: a standard bag or a ducted port for a dedicated system. Pair it with Makita’s AWS technology and pulling the trigger wirelessly activates a compatible vacuum—an easy, thoughtful upgrade for shop workflow.

Prior to using this saw, I read that some users had issues with the out-of-the-box accuracy of the table in relation to the blade. This situation is problematic when cutting trim, for instance, because it needs to fit perfectly.

I personally experienced none of that. I cut a variety of woods with this saw—from 2x10s to MDF trim—and the results completely satisfied me. Cuts were clean, splinter-free, and above all, accurate at connection.

The saw is powerful, thanks in part to its brushless motor and impressive battery, which Milwaukee claims makes 330 cuts per charge, but I honestly ran out of wood before that number (and according to the battery indicators, I still had half a charge remaining).

Milwaukee puts a lot of effort into getting its shadow line system clear and precise, and I appreciate that when it comes to eyeing up my cuts. As an added bonus, I find the LED field is the best of any saw I’ve used, cordless or otherwise. My only complaints are that the rear bevel is a little clunky to maneuver and the table extenders have an underwhelming feel to them. If you’re expanding your Milwaukee cordless platform, this saw is a great add.

A few of our readers gave us grief earlier this year for overlooking Evolution’s jobsite table saw on our list of the best table saws, so I called one in. I ran a piece of old angle iron through it before proceeding to cut hardwood, plywood, and pine trim with minimal tearout. My takeaway was that the saw lived up to the hype. Now, I’m curious how Evolution’s 10-inch miter saw handles the same materials.

I’ll start with framing lumber and trim to see how accurately the saw repeats miters and how cleanly it cuts in both bevel directions. Then, I’ll cut some aluminum angle stock and light-gauge steel tubing before moving on to hardwood with the same blade. I want to see how much cleanup each piece of metal needs and whether that last pair of hardwood miters fits together as neatly as the first pair of standard lumber and pine base molding. All throughout, I’ll be looking at standard saw features, as well, including motor power, build quality, table detents, LED lighting or shadow lines, and dust collection.

The three main types of miter saws are compound, dual compound, and sliding. Each variation performs specific functions and cuts better than the others, so it’s important that you understand their differences and also have a decent idea of how you plan on using your saw.

In addition to lowering straight down for perpendicular crosscuts, the blade of a compound miter saw also pivots from side to side for angled “miter” cuts, and it tilts to one side for bevel cuts. A “compound” cut utilizes both of these functions in one motion and is commonly used to create things like picture frames or to cut crown molding for installation.

Instead of tilting to only one side for bevel cuts, dual compound saws (also called “double” or “double-bevel” compound saws) tilt in both directions. This makes work much faster than using a standard compound saw because while a compound saw technically makes all the same cuts as a dual compound saw, its single-bevel design means you spend more time flipping workpieces around to cut opposite angles.

These two non-sliding types are solid options for homeowners who want a reasonably compact and portable machine.

A standard compound miter saw drops straight down onto the board. It’s great for narrow stock but limited by the diameter of the blade. A sliding compound miter saw adds rails that let the blade travel forward and backward during the course of the cut. This feature dramatically increases the width of material the saw can handle—making it possible to cut wider boards in a single pass. If you’re cutting a lot of shelving, flooring, or wide trim, a sliding miter saw, such as the DeWalt 20V MAX XR Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, is usually worth the extra cost and size.

When shopping for a miter saw, you’ll also need to decide what type of power source you prefer.

Cordless miter saws have improved dramatically over the last few years, mostly due to the evolution of high-capacity lithium-ion batteries and the inclusion of brushless motors. Today’s 18- and 20-volt models offer plenty of power for trim work and general carpentry without sacrificing the portability that makes cordless power tools appealing in the first place.

I like knowing I can set up the saw anywhere and get to work without worrying about finding power or running an extension cord through an open door or window. That said, corded saws still hold the edge when it comes to cutting ability and run time.

Most miter saws come with 10- or 12-inch blades, and that difference has a big impact on what type of cuts and tasks the saw excels at.

A 10-inch saw, such as the Metabo HPT Single Bevel Compound Miter Saw, is typically lighter and easier to move around your shop or from room to room. It’s more than capable of cutting trim, flooring, and smaller dimensional lumber.

A 12-inch saw, on the other hand, gives you significantly more cutting capacity—especially when you’re working with wider boards or tall trim pieces like crown molding. 12-inch saws, like our Best Overall choice, the Bosch GCM12SD Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, are a bit more awkward to move around the workplace.

A large saw also adds bulk and takes up more room in the shop or truck. But the trade-off to those negatives is that you’re far less likely to run into a job that you simply can’t handle. I’d rather deal with the extra footprint than discover upon starting a project that my saw is undersized. If you have the space, it’s often better to size up.

Blade speed, measured in rpm (revolutions per minute), is another important performance indicator. Most miter saws operate between 3,000 and 5,500 rpm, and naturally, higher speeds increase your cutting efficiency. Some saws, like the Hilti Nuron 22V miter saw, even allow you to customize your speed to a specific task, which makes it uniquely versatile.

That said, the relationship between the saw blade diameter and rpm makes comparing the speed of two miter saws a little more complex. Two saws running at the same rpm, but using different-sized blades—let’s say 7¼-inch and 12-inch—will not cut at the same speed. That’s because even though the center of each blade is spinning at the same speed, the outer edge of the 12-inch blade will turn faster than the edge of the 7¼-inch one.

Things get even more complicated when we bring the blade’s tooth count into the mix, with higher-tooth blades reducing speed. As a beginner, you can drive yourself a little crazy trying to determine the perfect combination of blade factors, so I’d recommend relying on your saw’s instruction manual for basic guidance.

Modern miter saws often include features designed to help you cut more accurately and consistently. Some use laser guides to project the cut line, while others use LED systems that cast a shadow from the blade, so you can see exactly where it will land. Detents at common angle stops around the saw table—like 22.5 degrees and 45 degrees—also make it faster to dial in repeated cuts. These features aren’t essential, but they make a noticeable difference when you’re making dozens of cuts in a row.

Paul Russell Smith is a former NYC ironworker turned screenwriter (Grace Point) and home renovation specialist. He lives in a crooked old farmhouse in Stockton, NJ, where he’s just as likely to be clearing a clogged pipe as rewriting a third act. When he’s not working, he enjoys hiking, pedestrian beer, and cooking over a live fire. His self-proclaimed spirit animal is the English Bulldog.

#6262. Pakistan’s first astronaut heads for China’s space station

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

At 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

Later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

That evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

One seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 4:35 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Thursday, at 7:05 p.m. EST, Rocket Lab will launch Night Owls Never Sleep on an Electron from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula.The payload is a StriX satellite for the Japanese company Synspective. StriX satellites use synthetic aperture radar to image the ground through clouds and darkness.

On Friday, Nov. 27, CASC is targeting 8:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

On Saturday, Nov. 28, CAS Space, a commercial launch company backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, plans to launch a Kinetica 1 at 8:00 p.m. EST from a sea platform in the South China Sea, supported by the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport, per Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Saturday, at 10:50 p.m. EST, a Long March 6C is slated to lift off from Taiyuan, according to Next Spaceflight. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Finally, at 11:39 p.m. EST on Saturday, SpaceX returns to SLC-4E for USSF-380, another classified Space Force mission. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

Closing out the week on Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the late Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of science and supplies to the ISS.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:51 p.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from Taiyuan carrying Shijian-24. China has not said what the satellite does; CGTN reported only that it reached its planned orbit.

On Friday, Nov. 20, at 6:59 a.m. EST, a Long March 8A launched from the commercial launch site at Wenchang with the 30th batch of satellites for Guowang, China’s state-backed broadband megaconstellation.

That night, at 11:20 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg, two days later than planned. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

The week closed on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 7:23 a.m. EST, when a Falcon 9 lifted off from the same pad with the National Reconnaissance Office’s NROL-136, a day later than planned. The launch came 32 hours after USSF-317, SpaceX’s fastest turnaround between launches from the same pad. The booster flew back to Landing Zone 4.

South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD), the military research arm of its defense ministry, is still preparing the first full demonstration flight of its solid-fueled Mir rocket from an offshore platform near Jeju Island. After canceling a June 30 attempt over safety concerns, the ministry has said only that it aims to launch by the end of the year.

ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), also has a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan on the books no earlier than November 2026. Its payload has not been announced.

#6261. A brain region known for listening helps us speak

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Recordings reveal how Wernicke’s area helps turn thoughts into words

A small bit of brain has big roles in understanding and producing speech, a new study finds.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

#6258. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#6257. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

M. Martin et al. Ubiquitously efficient solo navigation in group-living meerkats. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252200

Meghan Rosen is a senior writer who reports on the life sciences for Science News. She earned a Ph.D. in biochemistry and molecular biology with an emphasis in biotechnology from the University of California, Davis, and later graduated from the science communication program at UC Santa Cruz.
